Joohi Jimenez-Shahed studies movement disorders, neuromodulation and brain circuit therapeutics at the Icahn School of Medicine at Mount Sinai in New York City.

Big improvements in Parkinson’s disease treatment have been few and far between. The tantalizing prospect of regenerative stem-cell therapies to address this neurodegenerative condition is therefore creating considerable excitement.

A core component of Parkinson’s is the loss of dopamine-producing neurons, which normally provide carefully controlled neurotransmitter signals to the brain’s movement circuits1. This leads to people having substantial difficulties performing routine activities.

A dopamine-replacement approach provided one of the first major advances in Parkinson’s treatment2. Levodopa, a chemical precursor to dopamine that was introduced in the 1960s, treats symptoms effectively. But the levodopa honeymoon can be short. As the effect duration of each dose wanes, extra doses or medications are required to keep dopamine levels from falling. And the drug can come with a complication that many patients dread — writhing, uncontrolled involuntary movements known as dyskinesia. A surgical approach called deep brain stimulation (DBS) can mitigate these complications effectively3.

The downsides of levodopa raise a question: rather than replacing dopamine, why not replace the cellular machinery that produces it? Enter the dopaminergic stem cell. Engineered from cells sampled from an adult’s own tissues (known as autologous) or from a different individual (allogeneic), induced-pluripotent stem cells can be safely transplanted into human brains and can improve movement-related Parkinson’s symptoms, such as tremors, stiffness and slowness, without worsening dyskinesia4.

Only a few dozen people have received this experimental treatment. Major brain surgery is required to transplant the cells. Allogeneic cell transplants also require recipients to undertake a year of immunosuppression to ensure that the cells survive. Autologous cell transplants avoid this, but it takes 6–8 months to produce the cells for each patient.

It is not yet known how cell therapies will measure up to current standards of care. Early studies have been in people with advanced disease. At this stage, the chance of benefit might be reduced: the cells are implanted into an already degenerating circuit that could be difficult to restore.

Critics might therefore argue that dopamine cell therapies cannot produce a more robust effect than levodopa or DBS without imposing excess cost or risk. But the way that Parkinson’s treatments are investigated and approved can neither fully support this pessimistic view nor provide sufficient evidence for a more optimistic one.

Therapeutic development for Parkinson’s has mainly aimed to relieve symptoms. A more ambitious goal would be to slow the disease’s progression by altering its underlying biology. Yet there are substantial obstacles to developing such a treatment.

Implicit to the concept of disease modification is the need for a biomarker that measures the underlying biological processes5. Although a biological definition of Parkinson’s is emerging, it applies mainly to the identification of early disease. Relatively little is known about how such markers evolve in Parkinson’s, or how they relate to clinical progression6.

Long-term, multi-site observational studies such as the Parkinson’s Precision Medicine Initiative (see go.nature.com/4ayapbI) provide an ideal framework for exploring digital, biological and imaging markers, while benchmarking disease progression. Their success depends on building and sustaining large consortia, and on a healthy dose of time and effort from researchers and study participants, but the studies are constrained by funding inequities.

Even if such biomarkers were already at researchers’ disposal, there is no specific guidance from the US Food and Drug Administration on developing disease-modifying treatments7. The agency’s Regenerative Medicine Advanced Therapy designation speeds up cell- and gene-therapy development and approval. But eligibility requires only the intent to treat, modify, reverse or cure a serious disorder. As a result, clinical trials of regenerative therapies are likely to be designed to show benefits to a person’s symptoms without incurring the added cost and burden of showing a change in biology — a pragmatic but less ambitious path.

Crucially, supportive evidence for the broader potential of dopaminergic cell therapies is what will define their advantage. Cell dose, optimal treatment timing and objective evidence of cell survival, engraftment and effects on brain-network function would demonstrate whether cell therapies can produce lasting change in people with Parkinson’s. Public–private research partnerships could refine the required measurement tools and generate such data.

The ability to transform stem cells into dopamine-producing neurons and transplant them safely into human brains is momentous. Its use as a treatment extends an opportunity to chart another course for people with Parkinson’s by limiting levodopa complications and possibly the need for DBS. This outcome would bolster the hopes of people with this condition. But the real therapeutic breakthrough will occur only when scientists and regulators converge to advance the goal of restoring neural circuitry and function. That would be a truly bold step towards conquering this this relentless disease.

#1083. Man City's slump cannot be excused by guilty verdict: Too many blunders, too much arm waving and football problems are piling up after 3-1 defeat by Nottingham Forest, writes JACK GAUGHAN

Published: 14:52 EDT, 7 November 2026 | Updated: 15:31 EDT, 7 November 2026

This run will not be about the verdicts. This cannot be about the verdicts. Footballers do not care about these things, the stuff out of their control. Besides, all of them are earning cut-price transfers elsewhere were Manchester City to suffer relegation anyway. And cut-price fees mean bulkier salaries.

So to them the current climate, the circumstances around City – their recent history and their immediate future – does not overly matter. Sure, there might be the odd one who is slightly more philosophical and inquisitive about appeals and appendices but the majority won't be giving it much or any thought.

City insist on their innocence publicly and privately; until that changes, their players and Enzo Maresca carry on regardless. There were the usual jeers here, there were ditties about cheating, but that surely cannot affect them.

Instead, the performances over the past few weeks, this a third consecutive Premier League defeat and now sinking six points adrift of Arsenal, cannot be excused by the findings of an independent commission. The problems are football problems.

This is a squad who appear uncertain about specific aspects of their game. Namely how to build from the back – and that is prompting individual mistakes. It happened against Ipswich Town and at Aston Villa. On the river Trent, it was no different.

The statistics say City dominated another game and they deserved more but the eyes tell another story.

Man City are a squad who now appear uncertain about specific aspects of their game

The statistics say City dominated another game and they deserved more but the eyes tell another story

Three defeats in a row have seen Enzo Maresca's side slip six points behind leaders Arsenal

Too many errors. Too much arm waving. Too much feeling sorry for themselves when decisions go elsewhere. Oliver Glasner is not stupid, he will have seen examples of this play out in parts of City's victories as well as reverses.

As Liam Delap raced into the corner to celebrate his second with 17 minutes left – a huge day in his career against the club which moulded him – Glasner was dashing down the touchline with unbridled joy.

Nottingham Forest (5-2-2-1): Sels 6; Munoz 6 (Netz 65, 6), Cunha 8, Milenkovic 8, Murillo 7, Williams 8; Yates 8 (Sangare 79), Schlager 8; McAtee 7 (Ndoye 65, 6), Gibbs-White 7; Delap 9 (Jesus 87)

Man City (4-1-4-1): Donnarumma 5; Khusanov 5, Dias 5, Guehi 4 (Nunes 46, 7), Gvardiol 4 (O'Reilly 46, 6); Anderson 5; Ndiaye 6, Cherki 6, Fernandez 4 (Foden 78), Doku 6; Haaland 5

Forest displays have deserved more than their points total so far and this was vindication for their fifth manager in 14 months. Delap was exceptional, some personal redemption after criticism.

The way in which Glasner nudged James McAtee further forward, stationed higher from the off in order to pressurise the visitors, spoke to an idea that City arrived here ready to be ruffled and have been wearing a look of fragility.

By the time this was eight minutes shy of half time and McAtee was nicking possession from Elliot Anderson, drawing a foul that sparked another onslaught on Gianluigi Donnarumma's box, Forest were already two clear – and had been for some time. Phil Foden warmed up on the touchline, laughing and hugging with Callum Hudson-Odoi.

Forest preyed on City insecurities. A midfield structure that is simply not working at the moment, easily railroaded. A defence allergic to the basics and an epidemic of individual mistakes – either as a result of nervousness or blase attitude on the ball.

Straight to the mistakes. A real collection, these: the first in the fifth minute and the others 13 minutes afterwards. Jair Cunha wheeled away after picking Josko Gvardiol's pocket, meandering forward into the box and side-footing into the far corner largely unchallenged. Gvardiol seemed to have the air of a man who felt invincible when gathering possession before being eased off it.

Later, as Delap thundered forward 45 yards unchecked to hammer past Donnarumma, you wondered about the communication between these City players. Anderson and Iliman Ndiaye left things to each other near halfway, Xaver Schlager gave his thanks – finding Delap – and the City academy graduate bulldozed clear. Marc Guehi waved him through, Ruben Dias dithered and Maresca bowed his head.

Liam Delap was exceptional for Nottingham Forest, some personal redemption after criticism

Remarkably, this was the first time in seven years that City had gone two down inside 18 minutes

Remarkably, this was the first time in seven years that City had gone two down inside 18 minutes. Dias looked aghast at Guehi, who was then hooked at the break alongside Gvardiol. Erling Haaland and Rayan Cherki both stood in the centre circle, hands on hips.

It later emerged via replays that Anderson had been arguing with Abdukodir Khusanov in the build-up to Forest's opener as well, proof that City were nowhere near close to producing what was expected when on the ball in their own half.

Glasner had the weapons at his disposal to make this work but even the Austrian must have been surprised at the way in which they tickled City's soft underbelly. They had not scored at the City Ground all season. All change when owner Evangelos Marinakis made his first trip to see a game since Glasner's appointment, which felt particularly handy.

Anger permeated the eyes of some City players as the whistle went. Cherki stormed down the tunnel, animatedly discussing how to play through Forest with Fernandez when they re-emerged.

Their lifeline came after 52 minutes, a Ryan Yates deflection from Jeremy Doku's cross sitting up for Cherki to hammer home a half-volley off the bar. Doku soon almost squeezed another effort past Matz Sels and the mood shifted, City briefly creeping menacingly like the monsters they are portrayed as.

Maresca had introduced Matheus Nunes and Nico O'Reilly, with both affecting the upturn. An admission of selection errors, perhaps, although O'Reilly is managing an ongoing back issue and is set for therapy on it over the international break.

City will need some of that as a collective. Delap won the ball inside his own third, gliding past Anderson, and Forest's explosive counter ended with Delap spearing a shot in off the post after Morgan Gibbs-White carried possession unopposed for 60 yards. Delirium, Glasner darting to the corner flag.

The quirk of this is that City's failings mean Manchester United drop into the bottom three.

#1079. Chasing dynasty: How Gotham FC's NWSL Shield win completes transformation ahead of playoffs

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

En route to their second NWSL championship in two years, relatively new Gotham FC recruit Jaedyn Shaw was uninterested in the narratives that underestimated her team. The surprise win at the NWSL Shield-winning Kansas City Current in the playoff quarterfinals was not a surprise to her, and she made it clear with three quick words: "Underdog, my ass."

Shaw had a point on that cold day in the Midwest, and almost exactly a year later, it still stands. Gotham are the NWSL's new dynasty, and their Shield win marked their fifth major title in three years, with a sixth in their sights as the playoffs begin this weekend. The transformation was rapid for a team that has historically been a bottom-dweller, so much so that their 2023 championship triumph was a genuine surprise. They quickly built a title-winning team and reaped the rewards just as swiftly, but even as the muscle memory of title charges returns, Gotham will go about their next NWSL playoff journey differently. The target is officially on their backs, the onus officially on them to live up to the billing.

Gotham have played the vast majority of their playoff games as the lowest-seeded team in the postseason, winning the championship twice in those circumstances. Sunday's quarterfinal against the Seattle Reign, though, will be the first game they play as the unquestionable favorites to win the whole thing. How Gotham will play with the weight of expectations is entirely unclear, since they have never done it before, but it is a good problem of their own creation, one they have chased since the 2023 triumph.

Date: Sunday, Nov. 8 | Time: 12:30 p.m. ETLocation: Sports Illustrated Stadium -- Harrison, N.J.TV: ABC | Live stream: ESPN AppOdds: Gotham FC -150; Draw +265; Seattle Reign +340

Their blitz in the free-agent market in the winter of 2024 laid the foundation for their dynastic run, but the most fascinating feature of Gotham's years-long run of success is the evolution they have undergone since. U.S. women's national team defender Tierna Davidson has become the team's captain, her progressive passing ability making her a key fixture in head coach Juan Carlos Amoros' system. Her club and country teammate Rose Lavelle has become a standout, but the star of the show has been Shaw, who has barely missed a beat since her arrival in September 2025.

Shaw has 14 goals and seven assists in 35 NWSL games with Gotham, her wide-ranging skill set fully on display in Amoros' team. She has been a little bit of everything for the team's attack, which is arguably too reliant on her talents, but it is almost hard to fault Amoros for the approach. The system has allowed Shaw to flourish, in particular bringing out a clear goal-scoring quality that is key to a Gotham team that values defensive work rate first.

"First, I think the commitment they have to defend and the commitment they have to work hard for the team despite being some of the best players technically in the planet," Amoros said about both Shaw and Lavelle after a win over the Chicago Stars in September. "I think that helps the connection, not only between them two. There is a mutual respect there because of that but then also from the whole team. When you have to play and those are the players that produce the chances for us in the final third but then the people that [are] behind them are always supportive of them because of the work they put in and then we try to work a lot with them to how we can find them and how they can connect more with each other and the same with Sam [Kerr]."

He has found a unique way to make Shaw and Lavelle work together, despite the fact that they appear to have overlapping skill sets when it comes time for USWNT head coach Emma Hayes to slot them into her lineup. The pair often play just behind Kerr, an out-and-out striker, and assume the role of strikers themselves while balancing their creative tendencies. They have filled in some gaps along the way -- Kerr, for example, ranks third in the league with 9.67 expected goals since returning to the NWSL on July 16 but has scored just four times. Kerr does, though, have four assists in 17 games, one fewer than Shaw and one more than Lavelle over that span.

The connection between Lavelle and Shaw has offered Gotham a level of dynamism that has been missing in their attack at times over the years, even as they racked up title after title. It helps that the two have enjoyed working alongside each other, the 21-year-old Shaw in particular taking inspiration from Lavelle, a decade her senior.

"I think her movement is some of the best in the world, honestly," Shaw said after that September win over the Stars. "She's able to make stretch runs, drag players. She attracts so many players, opening up space for other players to get on the ball and then getting on the second one, I think, is one of her strengths and is something I'm trying to replicate off of her. I think she's just incredibly smart in soccer knowledge."

For each of them, a return to fitness after small injuries in the final weeks of the regular season comes not a moment too soon. Kerr's inconsistency is not the only attacking issue they will need to overcome -- Jordyn Dudley will miss the postseason with a foot fracture she sustained last month, her impressive rookie season coming to a close with four goals and three assists. Lavelle and Shaw will be particularly useful against the Reign, whose defensive qualities continue to be a strength.

Shaw has become the focal point of Gotham's reinvention in recent years, but Amoros' side has added experienced options in a wide variety of positions since the 2023 championship. The vast majority of Gotham's likely starters on Sunday will have joined the club after the 2023 playoff run, a steady stream of important players signing themselves up since. Ann-Katrin Berger, the 2024 goalkeeper of the year, made the move not long after Davidson and Lavelle did, and European champion Jess Carter followed right after. Midfielder Jaelin Howell, who has been in and around the USWNT, was recruited in time for the 2025 season, and Shaw joined months later. Left back Guro Reiten has two goals and six assists since making her club debut in April, while Kerr made the move at roughly the same time as midfielder Denise O'Sullivan, a two-time NWSL champion with the North Carolina Courage.

Gotham's reinvention is constant, the core evolving each and every season. It is a unique route to the top, but in another season of change, they found the consistency they have been chasing since the 2023 championship. The underdog label has well and truly been shed, the team chasing another tag entirely -- a third championship would put them level with the Portland Thorns as the most successful team in the league's history.

#1077. Kai Havertz leads the Premier League in offsides as Arsenal pile up infractions in 1-0 win over Hull City

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

LONDON -- Though there was some to-ing and fro-ing as to the order in which the offenses should be considered, it seemed fitting that what would have been Arsenal's best scoring chance of the first half of their 1-0 win over Hull City was wiped out for an offside. Here is a team whose attack has been drifting so out of sync that promising situations fall apart without the opponent needing to get involved.

Sometimes the opponent is even willing to offer them a helping hand. Only the members of the International Football Association Board might be able to say for sure whether Arsenal should have had a penalty when Kai Havertz's shirt was pulled by Hull City's Nobel Mendy as Bruno Guimaraes took a long-range shot. The striker was impeded, but he had been standing in an offside area. Was he attempting to play the ball when Mendy grabbed hold of his jersey? If not, then the foul should have taken precedence and Arsenal should have had a penalty. Instead, they had to wait until the 72nd minute for their win, Martin Odegaard bundling in the rebound off Noni Madueke's shot.

At least that meant Mikel Arteta could jokingly say he had not seen the spot kick that might have been. There may be a question about that particular penalty and offside, but the big-picture statistics are mind-boggling, such that there surely has to be some air in these numbers.

In the last seven Premier League seasons, no team has averaged more than three offsides per game. Only Burnley in 2021-22 and Liverpool two years later have averaged more than 2.5, in the process reaching over 100 for the season. In their 10th game of the season, Arsenal committed offside offenses Nos. 32, 33, 34 and 35. At the final whistle, that was 11 more than any other team in the league, and there is a very real prospect that lead does not get eaten into. Field a team of Pippo Inzaghis and you'd do well to put up these numbers.

There has to be something to this, right?

What makes this all the more curious is that Arsenal have not been a team that particularly struggled to stay onside before this season. In the previous six campaigns, they were caught about as often as the average Premier League team when you adjust for possession. When these relatively low-volume statistics warp like this, at least part of the answer is going to be variance. A bit more of it might be that Arsenal have a 10-game sample size that includes Aston Villa. Still, that sample is over a quarter of the season. Arsenal have had a string of games where they have been caught offside with frequency.

This looks like a problem. Even Arteta acknowledged that. "There are many areas that we need to improve. That's one, that's related sometimes to the timing or the situation, or really the position [of the opponent], where he's lined up and what space he's given you.

"Certainly it's far too many. It's true that the Villa game obviously he's putting those stats in a different perspective. I think the sample is quite short to analyse it, but you have a point there."

As for the Villa game, Mikel, yes, that's eight of your 35. Leeds is seven, though. Coventry five, Hull four. These are all well above the Premier League average. The chief culprit for this spate of infractions is certainly Havertz. His 15 offsides are not just seven more than any other player in the top flight; they are more than any Arsenal player committed in the entirety of last season's title campaign.

Again, this feels a little unprecedented. In the six seasons prior to this one, Havertz ranked 48th among forwards in the division for how frequently they were caught offside. The worst offenders, your Ashley Barneses, Darwin Nunezes and Cristiano Ronaldos, might get flagged once every 70 or 80 minutes. Havertz hovered around the 140 mark. This season it's not far off once per half.

Has he lost some burst? Gradient Sports' physical data would suggest he is moving about as swiftly this season as any other. A broader view is that this attack might have greater joy punishing high lines with more pacey options in it. For a player who makes so many runs off the ball, Madueke is caught offside relatively infrequently (though his was one of the four today). That is probably because he can give his man a yard in a way that Havertz or even Bukayo Saka, third in the league with seven offsides, can't quite.

Have defenses sussed Havertz's movement out? That doesn't seem entirely clear, not least given that Hull misjudged their line more than once, allowing Havertz in a one-on-one position where he should have done much better than cut the ball onto Mendy's trailing leg.

Arteta's explanation is simple. "It's all about timing," he said. "So there is a signal on the ball, and you need to time it around that. If that's a second too late or half a second too late, that's all."

Certainly Arsenal could release the ball a bit quicker. If there is a flaw in the game of Odegaard, whose nine passes to an offside teammate also lead the league, it is that he tends to want that one extra touch. That much was apparent in the win at Aston Villa, when the captain had the ideal chance to slip Havertz through in position to bend one in the far post. He took three touches when two would have sufficed, and it was all a moment too late.

Bruno Guimaraes (four such passes) is in a similar vein. And perhaps Arsenal as a club are a bit too much of that ilk. Does the specter of Alex Hleb and Samir Nasri still haunt this team? Arteta might have said as much, that the thing about Arsenal is they always try to walk it in.

"We need to find ways to be more efficient, sometimes even more pragmatic," he said. "Sometimes my feeling is that we are trying to score a perfect goal against these low blocks. We need to be much more chaotic than that."

You can see that in some of those offsides above, especially the smattering around the right flank that Arsenal like to make their creative hub. It's the attempted reverse balls, the quick one-twos and slide-rule passes to a teammate on the overlap. Offside No. 36 might well have been another of those, an overlapping run from Jurrien Timber where Madueke released the pass a beat too late and the Dutchman stopped rather than cede Hull a free kick.

Instead, Madueke proved the value of an alternative approach right throughout this match. Driving at his fullback time and time again, he manufactured positions where things might happen without having to worry about a give-and-go or timing his run correctly. In an age where so many opponents, including Hull, are more intent on gumming up their opposition than gritting and grinding, a bit of unpredictability from one of Arsenal's own players goes a long way. As for the offsides, of course that feels like a problem, a lot of possessions wasted by Arsenal players' own inability to get on the right beat. It has been. It does not mean it is going to be. Injuries mean that Havertz and Odegaard have rarely shared the pitch over the last few seasons. Get them and Saka together for weeks on end and the old rhythm will come back to them, and this should be nothing more than a weird, if intriguing, blip.

Three different managers have been sacked in that time, and the mood in north London had plunged to grim lows, but finally there is a sense that something truly exciting is stirring at the Tottenham Hotspur Stadium.

This victory over Crystal Palace was not as impressive as last week’s triumph at Chelsea, but it did not need to be. They did so with relative ease, taking complete control of possession and creating endless goalscoring opportunities.

Roberto De Zerbi’s team ended the night with 34 shots to Palace’s two and with 758 completed passes to Palace’s 149. The goals ultimately came from two defenders, Archie Gray and Jan Paul van Hecke, but there was a long list of Spurs players who might have scored here.

Even in the two games Palace have won, against Fulham and Nottingham Forest, they were lucky to do so. The likes of Sean Dyche and Thomas Frank, both of whom would be strong candidates to replace Sage if Palace do pull the trigger, will no doubt have been keeping an eye on events here.

The decision for Palace chairman Steve Parish, then, is whether this result represented a continuation of the team’s problems or was an aberration caused by the early red card. While Tottenham are chasing a third successive league victory for the first time in 616 day, De Zerbi insisted there will be no complacency. “For me nothing has changed. Pierre Sage, the Palace manager, lightened the load after knocking Fulham out of the Carabao Cup in midweek but seemed surprised that the fans have remained so supportive. “It’s always a good sign,” he said. “I appreciate it [singing his name at Craven Cottage] very much and I can thank them but I prefer they are with the team than me alone. Asked what he has learnt about fan sentiment from looking at social media, he said: “I think they understood what happened, why we are not perfect at the moment. #1073. Finland, the world's happiest nation, faces a glum winter

Finns have many reasons to feel content, but the country's pile of debt is not one of them. Russia's war in Ukraine has added to the fiscal burden. Can the Nordic nation absorb another shock?

There's an uneasy mood in Finland, the country that's ranked the world's happiest for nine consecutive years. A colder-than-usual winter is on the way and so is the toughest austerity budget in years.

With an election due in April, the argument is no longer how much to cut, but which services, benefits and pensions will face the biggest cuts.

Finland's debt and deficit levels are in their worst state since the 1990s, when a banking crash and the collapse of the Soviet Union — a key export partner — pushed the Nordic nation into its own Great Depression.

Last month, Finland's national statistical institution confirmed that the national debt had reached 90.3% of gross domestic product (GDP) in the second quarter. Before the pandemic, that figure was around 65%.

Trouble to the east is, again, part of the reason. Finland ramped up defense spending after joining NATO a year after Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine. Helsinki, which used to rely on Moscow for about a third of its energy, also faced much higher costs as it transitioned to other suppliers.

The Finnish government has spent more than it earns since the 2008/9 global financial crisis, partly due to an aging population and sluggish economic growth. Last month, the State Treasury projected the fiscal deficit would reach 4.2% of GDP in 2026.

Brussels has piled pressure on Helsinki to bring down the borrowing gap, as European Union rules require member states to stay below 3% of GDP. In January, the European Council opened an excessive deficit procedure and gave Finland until the end of 2028 to reach the desired target.

Prime Minister Petteri Orpo's government, which took office in June 2023, said it would aim to save about €9 billion ($10.1 billion) during this parliamentary term. But whoever wins the next election will have to cut much deeper, economists warn.

"The amounts currently estimated range from €8 to €11 billion," Jarkko Kivisto, an advisor to the Bank of Finland's monetary policy and research department, told DW.

Earlier this year, all but one political party agreed to support a debt brake, where the next government commits to tightening the country's deficit to about 2% of GDP by 2031.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

To date, Orpo's center-right National Coalition is the only party to promise a further €9 billion in cuts if he wins a second term. As well as further savings from health, social care and welfare, Orpo also plans to target workplace pensions, without reducing current payouts.

While the Social Democrats plan to split the reforms between spending cuts and tax hikes, Orpo plans to achieve his target without raising taxes — meaning public services will bear the brunt.

Kivisto, however, cautioned: "The deficit is so large that it would need a package that includes tax increases and expenditure cuts."

While Finland's at-risk-of-poverty rate is lower than the EU average, unemployment is higher than anywhere else in the bloc. In August, Finland's jobless total stood at 10.3%, just above Spain's 10%, according to Eurostat, the bloc's statistics agency. Youth unemployment reached 23.3%, against an EU average of 15.4%.

With household spending already falling, Lauri Holappa, director of the Finnish Centre for New Economic Analysis, warned that a new round of austerity would be a hard blow for the domestic economy.

"More than a quarter of the population works in the public sector, so if those workers face the threat of being sacked, the savings rate will rise and private spending will drop again," Holappa told DW.

Successive pressures ranging from the COVID-19 pandemic, higher interest rates and the global financial impact of two current wars have hurt efforts to cut the growing gap between income and borrowing. The 2027 budget proposal still counts on a spending gap of €12.4 billion.

Before the Ukraine war, Finland had already committed to buying 64 F-35A fighter jets from the United States, in a deal worth about €8.4 billion.

During more than four years of Russia's war in Ukraine, the Nordic nation raised military spending from $4.5 billion to over $8 billion per year, according to the Stockholm International Peace Research Institute (SIPRI).

In April, the government said it would further increase defense spending to 3.2% of GDP, close to NATO's 3.5% target.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

With oil prices remaining close to $100 a barrel due to the Iran war, the government has so far resisted pressure to increase fuel subsidies. That's despite the Bank of Finland recording a 50% rise in the cost of imported energy in the early months of the Iran war.

While Finland’s shift to renewables, along with the opening of the Olkiluoto 3 nuclear power plant in 2023, has helped avoid a worse energy crisis, the central bank warned this summer that sustained high oil and gas prices would mean "lower economic growth and higher inflation" next year.

On another positive note, parts of Finland's export sector are booming, thanks to strong metal and shipbuilding orders, which Holappa described as strong as "the boom years of Nokia," when the once market-leading phone maker carried Finnish economic growth.

"There is a possibility that the export sector can steer us out of this recession," he told DW, as long as demand from the rest of Europe remains strong.

Despite the multiple roadblocks to bringing down the deficit, market reaction to Finland's debt woes has, so far, been muted. Rating agencies have kept the country's outlook stable, apart from S&P, which turned negative in April without cutting the rating.

On October 6, the premium the Finnish government pays over Germany to borrow for 10 years was 38 basis points. That compares to 128 for France and 107 for Italy. In other words, investors still treat Finnish debt as among the safest in Europe.

That is, as long as the next shock is not another extended oil-price spike, a fresh escalation from Russia, or a Europe-wide debt crisis centered on France.

Next March, Finland could still be named the planet's happiest nation for the 10th year in a row. How long the smiles last, once the bill for decades of borrowing arrives a month later, is anyone's guess.

See more of the month’s sharpest science shots, selected by Nature’s photo team.

An outbreak of anthrax has killed at least 30 hippos (Hippopotamus amphibius) in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) in the past month. No cases of the infectious disease have been reported in people so far. The wildlife outbreak puts further pressure on already limited resources, say researchers, as the DRC grapples with armed conflict and large outbreaks of Ebola and cholera.

Contributions to a United Nations-run pot for the conservation of nature — expected to raise US$1 billion per year — total just US$10,588 two years after it was established. The Cali Fund seeks voluntary contributions from companies that profit from genetic data collected from Earth’s biodiversity. So far, only five small biotech companies have contributed.

In the 2026 fiscal year, which ended on 30 September, the US National Science Foundation (NSF) funded fewer than 100 new social-science grants, compared with a historical average of roughly 850 per year. In dozens of programme areas, including economics and archaeology, the agency awarded no new grants at all. Earlier this year, the administration of President Donald Trump stated that it wants to eliminate the NSF’s social, behavioural and economic sciences (SBE) directorate altogether, leaving several decades-long projects hanging in the balance.

A study in mice might help explain the long-known fact that castration extends life span in most mammals, including people — and why men tend to live shorter lives than women. In the experiment, researchers removed the testicles of mice before puberty, after puberty or in old age, and found that all interventions increased median lifespan — with the late intervention leading to the biggest improvement. The findings suggest that testes’ apparently harmful effects begin later in life, rather than during their puberty heyday.

Widespread migration of people from countryside to cities is leading to a surprising drop in biodiversity in some of the low-intensity farming landscapes where humans have lived in harmony with other creatures for millennia. For example, in Japan, forests where farmers once cut trees for fuel and removed fallen leaves for fertilizer are becoming dense and closed in again — leading to losses in species such as fireflies and harvest mice. Volunteers have taken up saws to help, but experts say that longer-term solutions are needed, such as rewilding or addressing rural depopulation.

When Edward Freytag, a 66-year-old music teacher, injured his brain in a motorcycle crash, he developed the ability to instantly recognize musical notes. He’s the first person known to have acquired perfect pitch from a brain injury. In this beautifully illustrated feature, explore how our brains process sound, learn how Freytag’s injury might have affected him this way, and listen to a composition he wrote in a fugue-like state during the early stages of his recovery.

I’m lucky enough to cover many marvellous researchers and projects, but this award really lives up to its name: the work it recognizes is truly inspiring. Check it out.

#1070. Suzuki howler costs Aston Villa crucial points

Aston Villa goalkeeper Zion Suzuki went from being serenaded with a chorus of “world’s No 1” to making a bizarre blunder that denied Unai Emery’s side a third successive Premier League victory.

The Villa manager, however, preferred to focus on a string of important saves from Suzuki rather than the uncharacteristic mistake that allowed Fulham to collect a deserved point.

It all went wrong for the hosts just after the hour mark in a match where Fulham provided more than a few scares before finding the net in unexpected fashion.

Alex Iwobi, who had been denied superbly by a Suzuki save just moments earlier, swung in a corner. It was right on top of the Villa goalkeeper, who tried to keep it out but only succeeded in fumbling it over the line. A frantic attempt to gather the ball was in vain and goal-line technology confirmed the goal stood.

Zion Suzuki drops Alex Iwobi's corner and Fulham are level! 🫨 https://t.co/KwLFMRpKqk

Suzuki appeared to have been put off by the presence of Fulham’s Shea Charles, but Emery refused to single out the player for criticism.

“I prefer to speak about the saves that he made,” the Villa manager said. “This is part of football. I think he played fantastically and he is doing a lot of saves so he can make one mistake. It is part of football. We can be mature about this.

“I still want to see consistency. Over the last five Premier League matches, we are winning three and drawing two. It’s not bad but with our poor start it’s not enough.

“We have to change our mind quickly for Tuesday against Barcelona. We want to test ourselves at this level.”

Villa go to the Nou Camp with a 100 per cent Champions League record to their name this season. But they will need to improve on Saturday evening’s performance to get a result in Spain.

As well as Suzuki’s error, a 14th-minute penalty miss from John McGinn also proved costly.

It was awarded after Leon Goretzka, making his full league debut for Villa, saw his header hit Sander Berge’s raised hand. Nobody appealed at the time but referee Sam Barrott was sent to the touchline monitor by VAR to review the incident and gave the spot-kick.

McGinn’s attempt, however, hit the crossbar and the chance to take an early lead went begging. The Villa captain seemed a strange choice to take the spot-kick as he has only ever scored one career penalty, but Emery defended the choice, saying: “We analysed the penalty takers in the squad and it was McGinn here.”

Nicolas Jackson was on hand to ease Villa’s nerves before the break, though. the Villa manager had said before the game that the striker’s goalscoring capability meant he was capable of matching the likes of Harry Kane. Collecting Johan Manzambi’s superbly weighted pass, Jackson forced his way past two defenders before sliding in the goal that put Villa ahead.

Emery’s touchline celebrations said it all as the Senegal forward continues to flourish under the man who knew how to get the best out of him at Villarreal.

Nicolas Jackson scores his fifth league goal in five games! 🔥 https://t.co/W0xmFtW1Gt

Robinson put in another cross and Suzuki got a touch that was enough to make Garcia put his shot wide. Villa were living dangerously and the Japanese goalkeeper made another outstanding stop to keep out Iwobi’s header. But then it all went wrong for Suzuki when he fumbled Iwobi’s corner.

That allowed Fulham’s recent revival under manager, Alvaro Arbeloa, to continue – they now have seven points from their past three games.

“We spoke at half-time about what we had to do,” Arbeloa said. “If you want to win a game you have to fight and I think we have to believe in our way, we’ve shown we can beat anyone in the way that we play but we have to be aggressive.

Of all the daft statements to have come out of Aston Villa – and I am including Doug Ellis’s frequent claims that he invented the bicycle kick – it is hard to think of anything as absurd as suing a pundit for speaking the truth.

Jamie Carragher’s common-sense declaration that Villa manager Unai Emery might consider a move to Manchester United – because it is a bigger club – has apparently inflicted such a deep wound to the self-esteem of Nassef Sawiris, the chairman, that he has initiated a legal complaint.

“If we are thinking after the match against Fulham, then we are making a mistake and we are completely wrong,” Emery said. “We are prioritising the Premier League, and this is the message. To keep our consistency and demands means that each match is a test.”

Having failed to win any of their first six league games, Fulham have now won back-to-back Premier League games, with consecutive 1-0 wins over Hull and Coventry, which has lifted them out of the relegation zone.

“It [managing in England] is a very tough challenge but I am so happy to be here,” Alvaro Arbeloa said. “I am where I want to be and I am really enjoying my days. I want to win games and I think we are performing well but we need to improve.

#1068. Art for freedom: Maria Kalesnikava in Bonn

The Belarusian musician and civil rights activist Maria Kalesnikava held the keynote speech on the importance of art at the 2026 Beethovenfest in Bonn. She also visited DW.

Maria Kalesnikava knows all too well how authoritarian regimes repress art: The Belarusian flautist and activist spent five years in detention as a political prisoner, three of which were in solitary confinement. Speaking at this year's Beethovenfest, she said: "A person's external freedom can be taken away, sometimes almost entirely. Their freedom of movement, contacts with other people, and access to information can be limited." She pointed out that it is, however, much harder to control what has already become part of one's memory, imagination and inner experience. "And it is precisely in this that I find the explanation for why culture is so important for a free society and why authoritarian systems so often view it with distrust" she concluded during the keynote speech.

A key figure of the Belarusian opposition, the artist and political activist was arrested by the regime of Alexander Lukashenko in the summer of 2020, after the regime had violently suppressed the peaceful revolution for democracy and freedom. Across the country, mass protests and a democratic civil rights movement took place after the controversial presidential election on August 9, 2020.

Kalesnikava recalled how, during her imprisonment, she had carried her world and her experiences, with her all along. This enabled her to remain free, and not to feel like a victim. To Kalesnikava, this is precisely the power of art and also the reason why all dictators — whether Stalin, Hitler or Putin and Lukashenko — hate independent arts and culture, even if it's not overtly political.

During a panel discussion in Bonn, Kalesnikava stressed this point directly:

"The question often arises: what are we defending in Ukraine? Why do we need so much money and new weapons? For me, it is completely clear: the war Russia started is not just against Ukraine. It's a war against European values and European culture. It is a war against our civilization." Kalesnikava realized this immediately when she heard about the Russian war against Ukraine in February 2022, while she was imprisoned.

Kalesnikava was released and has been living in freedom again for ten months now — a miracle that she didn't think was possible and an achievement of international diplomacy. The fact that she emerged and returned to her life full of resilience is thanks in part to Beethoven and Bach, as Kalesnikava, who studied the flute and earned a degree in early and new music in Minsk and Stuttgart, recalled. "I spent a lot of time in complete silence. But this silence was almost never empty, because music constantly played in my head," Kalesnikava said in Bonn. "We musicians know this state very well — sometimes a melody or a musical phrase gets so stuck in your head that it's simply impossible to get rid of it. In normal life, this can even be annoying. In prison, I realized for the first time that this could bring great happiness."

During her visit to Bonn, the Belarusian activist also visited DW and appeared as a guest on the DW Russian language show "DW Novosti." Kalesnikava currently lives in Berlin following an invitation by the German government, where she is also recovering from the horrors she experienced. She sees it as her responsibility to remind the world about what is happening to more than 800 political prisoners in Belarus, as well as the importance and fragility of free artistic expression. On October 2, 2026, she held her keynote speech at the Beethovenfest in Bonn as part of a conference titled "Cultural Events as Political Spaces?," organized with the support of the German Federal Cultural Foundation.

More than 200 representatives from concert institutions and music festivals from across Germany came to the newly renovated Beethovenhalle in Bonn for the final weekend of this year's Beethovenfest. Together, they debated innovative forms and formats for music, as well as issues that stretch far beyond the music industry and urge on to think outside the box.

"Arts and culture are not responsible for taking on specific opinions from political parties, or for making explicitly political statements," Steven Walter, artistic director of the Beethovenfest and host of the conference, told DW. "What art always creates, however, is spaces for encounter, and places where people can tolerate ambivalence. And that is such an important part of our society, that we're able to handle making collective experiences." To Walter, this is precisely where arts and culture come in, as artists create spaces for independent thought, subjective interpretations, as well as doubts. "Perhaps it's true that there is something like a DNA of freedom in the nature of art," Walter explained in an interview with DW.

The festive closing of the 2026 Beethovenfest took place on 3 October, which is also German Unity Day. The BBC Philharmonic Orchestra, under the baton of conductor Anja Bihlmaier, performed Johannes Brahms' "A German Requiem," an iconic piece that evokes reconciliation and trust.

After four weeks of Beethovenfest 2026, the festival recorded the highest number of visitors in a decade. Around 35,000 people came to experience, celebrate and discuss art together at more than 100 concerts and events.

This article was written by Andrey Gorezky, translated from German and edited by Sarah Hucal and Tenzin Sekhon.

#1067. Non-league footballer in stable condition after collapsing in warm-up and rushed to hospital, leading to match being abandoned

By BEN WILLCOCKS, ASSISTANT SPORTS EDITOR

Published: 11:35 EDT, 7 November 2026 | Updated: 16:31 EDT, 7 November 2026

Truro City's match against Folkestone Invicta was abandoned due to a medical emergency on Saturday after a footballer collapsed during the warm-up.

Yassine En-Neyah, 26, was rushed to hospital in an ambulance after collapsing while preparing with his team-mates on the pitch. It was later confirmed he was in a stable condition.

The former Nottingham Forest academy youngster had been named among the substitutes to face Folkestone in the National League South game in Kent.

A club statement on Saturday read: 'Truro City can confirm that this afternoon's match against Folkestone Invicta has been postponed.

'Yassine En-Neyah required medical assistance during the warm-up and was transferred to the William Harvey hospital in Ashford for further treatment.'

The club added a welcome on Saturday night, saying: 'He is stable, sitting up and chatting, but will remain in hospital overnight under observation.

Truro City's clash with Folkestone Invicta has been abandoned due to a medical emergency

Yassine En-Neyah - pictured before the game - was named on the bench to face Folkestone

Club Statement:Truro City can confirm that this afternoon's match against Folkestone Invicta has been postponed. Yassine En-Neyah required medical assistance during the warm-up and was transferred to the William Harvey hospital in Ashford for further treatment.We will… pic.twitter.com/IyiF2VIFMz

'The club would like to place on record its thanks to Truro City's medical staff, their counterparts at Folkestone Invicta, along with all club personnel from the home club.

'Both the National League and Football Association have also offered their help and support. There have also been many well wishes from Truro City fans and the wider football community too.'

Truro City's players had earlier gathered around the rear of the ambulance where En-Neyah was being treated to shield him from view.

The Moroccan-born former Republic of Ireland youth international began his career at Nottingham Forest, making his professional debut in January 2020 as a substitute during an FA Cup third-round clash against Chelsea.

After being released by Forest in 2021, the winger has played for multiple non-league sides including Shelbourne, Waterford and Maldon & Tipree.

Having briefly represented Truro in 2023, En-Neyah returned to the Tinners for a second spell in 2024, where he has remained since.

When he signed his new Truro contract last season, En-Neyah admitted he didn't think twice about the decision to stay.

'Truro's been my home for the last couple of seasons and it was a very easy decision,' he told BBC Radio Cornwall.

'I feel home so I just want to continue working hard and help the club achieve greater things.

'It wasn't a case of having to think about it, it was just a matter of getting it done and continuing to work hard and do well for the club and for myself.'

#1066. Arsenal nous frustrates Liverpool as 14-year Anfield hoodoo ends with statement win

It is clear and obvious that Arsenal will be the team to beat in the Premier League title race, especially given that we do not yet know the fate of faltering Manchester City and their looming punishment.

A statement victory against Liverpool, their first in the league at Anfield since 2012, took Arsenal back to the top. And who would bet against them staying there and retaining their title?

Few would when they defend and manage a game – and it was game management in every sense – like this. From the formidable to the cynical – that was the statement. Against the Scousers, Arsenal had the nous.

“The mission was something we didn’t complete in 14 years,” Mikel Arteta said, having famously – in an Amazon documentary series – played You’ll Never Walk Alone to his players as they walked out to train to try and overcome a perceived mental block.

“There are reasons for that. Some of it psychological, some of it moments we did not nail on the pitch,” the Arsenal manager added of the winless run.

The result means that the north Londoners have already now won away at Villa Park, the Stadium of Light, the City Ground and Anfield. Stadiums where they dropped points last season. And that feels ominous.

A win would maybe have thrust Liverpool into the title race. Instead, under Andoni Iraola, and with an evolving young team – with promising 19-year-old midfielder Trey Nyoni handed his league debut – they are already nine points behind after just nine matches.

It is also clear, however, that they could have prevented this defeat having somehow been denied a first-half penalty after Alexander Isak’s shirt was blatantly pulled by Jurrien Timber as the striker tried to head home a cross.

Referee Andy Madley may have missed it, but what was the excuse of Stuart Attwell, the VAR? It was a stunningly poor decision – another bad day for Pro Ref and the use of technology.

It might be argued that Timber did not pull hard enough to prevent Isak from reaching the ball. But the defender grabbed the shirt and continued to hold it for a long time. It had to be a penalty. Little wonder Iraola said Isak should dive next time. Who can blame him?

What is also clear and obvious is that, once again, Arsenal’s resilience, defensive determination and appetite for toughing it out will be their greatest weapons. They are certainly, under Arteta, not here to win friends – just to win matches and trophies.

“That defensive line, that togetherness we have is undefeated. It’s something I have never seen before,” Declan Rice, who was also a stand-out performer and delivered a fine assist for the winner, said.

Arsenal’s version of the Yellow Wall was, indeed, hugely impressive – it is now six clean sheets from their nine league games and, despite all their pressure, Liverpool did not have a shot on target. That has never happened in the Premier League since such statistics started to be compiled in 2003 (422 games ago).

“That’s incredible. It did not feel like it on the pitch. Again, it’s the commitment of every single player,” Arteta said. And that was indisputable.

Even the expected second-half momentum, the expected surge of attack after attack as Liverpool faced the Kop, crashed on Arsenal’s back line. The visitors were so well-drilled that they stifled space – they refused to crumble.

Arsenal put their bodies on the line with blocks and tackles and a bit of time-wasting. There were dark arts, especially from both centre-halves with Gabriel going unpunished after claiming he was struck in the face by Isak early on – VAR anyone? – and the otherwise outstanding Ezri Konsa throwing himself to the ground after minimal contact from the Liverpool centre-forward.

In fairness there was also a bit of that from an increasingly frustrated Liverpool with Alexis Mac Allister going down after touching heads with Noni Madueke, having already tried to provoke Martin Odegaard with a hand to the head when the Arsenal captain was on the turf. That was not good from Mac Allister either.

And the only goal? Again, more frustration for Liverpool. It was well-constructed from Arsenal, but only after Alisson Becker’s loose goal kick, aimed towards Jérémy Jacquet, who was slow to react, was intercepted by Odegaard with Bruno Guimarães poking the ball to the right, where it was collected by Madueke.

There was an overlap by Rice and his low centre was precise and dangerous across the face of the six-yard area, with Virgil van Dijk unsure what to do. It ran beyond the far post where Kai Havertz side-footed home.

Here is a question I did not think I would be asking at any stage this season: will Liverpool win the Premier League?

It would be premature to describe this Sunday’s Anfield fixture as a title duel. Arsenal are better equipped to defend their crown, while Liverpool are a work in progress.

Whatever the outcome this weekend, Arsenal will leave Merseyside as the overwhelming favourites to claim back-to-back titles. They have a six-point lead over Liverpool. Should that extend to nine, Andoni Iraola’s primary objective coming into this season will remain unchanged; qualifying for the Champions League will represent a promising start to his reign.

What makes this weekend more significant is the champions will find a different Anfield to that which ended last season in such a downbeat mood, and came into this one uncertain of what was in store.

The discussion about what is achievable for Liverpool in the coming months is evolving by the week, the team bubbling along slightly under the radar.

There are several reasons why there are those who believe Iraola’s side might push Arsenal closer than anticipated.

Good afternoon and welcome to live coverage of the Premier League match between Liverpool, who start the game in fifth with 15 points, and Arsenal, six points in front of them in second place. Anfield, that glorious night in May 1989 excepted, has not been the happiest of hunting grounds for Arsenal and though their record there recently – three draws in the last four visits – has perked up, they have gone 13 seasons without a victory, so long ago, in fact, that Mikel Arteta was in the side that celebrated Lukas Podolski  and Santo Cazorla earning them a 2-0 win.

Having already lost within the perimeter of the historic county of Lancashire this week, when knocked out of the Carabao Cup on penalties by League Two Fleetwood Town, the champions will be keen to end that barren streak and go into the 4.30pm kick-off on the back of three successive league victories following their defeat by Brighton. Points today, one or three, will put them ahead of Manchester City at the top of the table while victory for Liverpool would allow them to overtake Chelsea and move one point behind Brighton, the team they beat last week with the kind of performance that inspired talk of a credible title campaign.

#1065. Author or artificial intelligence? Literature in crisis

AI is a hot topic at this year's Frankfurt Book Fair. An international literary scandal has raised questions about machine-generated texts.

It's the hot-button topic at the Frankfurt Book Fair: How profoundly will artificial intelligence (AI) transform the book industry, and how can this transformation be regulated?

Given the warnings about the technology's long-term risks to humanity as a whole, such debates might appear rather narrow in scope. In reality, however, they concern very concrete issues — copyright protection, the power of tech giants and the future of creativity. Many agree that the political measures taken don't go far enough.

This year, however, another aspect has entered the debate: Can we actually recognize when a text has been written with the help of artificial intelligence, and if so, can this be proven?

These are some of the questions raised by the current scandal surrounding Haitian-Canadian author Thelyson Orelien and his debut novel, "C'etait ca ou mourir," (This title means "It Was Either That or Die" in English but an English translation has not yet been published), which was published in Canada in the spring.

The book about global migration was universally acclaimed, with translation rights sold in more than 20 languages. Soon after the book was published in France, it was long-listed for the prestigious Prix Goncourt.

But then, all of a sudden, allegations emerged that the book had been written almost entirely using AI. Orelien, a rising literary star, found himself branded a fraud despite denying all the allegations. His nomination for the Goncourt was withdrawn.

So, who should we believe? An author or an AI that claims to have identified AI-generated writing?

"We will have to learn to live with doubt," said Hannes Bajohr, a professor of German literature at the University of California, Berkeley.

Bajohr has spent years examining how AI is changing both writing and reading. His prediction: If the origins of texts can no longer be reliably established, we will have to evaluate them differently. What matters will be their quality alone, rather than whether AI was used in the writing process.

Nina George, a bestselling author and the honorary president of the European Writers' Council, is unwilling to accept this.

At the Frankfurt Book Fair, she was awarded the Friedrich Perthes Prize in recognition of her commitment to issues such as AI and copyright reform.

George has addressed the European Parliament and the lower house of the German parliament, speaking and writing tirelessly about the dangers of AI models. It is perverse, she said, that an author should suddenly have to prove that their writing is the creation of a human. The focus of her campaigns are the tech corporations' self-serving mentality and copyright protection.

But what if an author sees AI not as an enemy but as a tool that makes writing easier?

US author and artist Luke Stoffel deliberately used AI in his memoir, "How To Win One Million Dollars and Shit Glitter," and was open about doing so.

"I'm dyslexic," he said in a video interview. "I've always written and made up stories, but I never dared to take them any further."

It was only with the help of AI, he said, that he was able to fulfill his dream. The technology drew his attention to weaknesses in his writing and suggested a marketing strategy that actually worked.

In May 2026, he received an award from the Independent Book Publishers Association for the book.

For South African author Coral Hart, AI is actually the foundation of her business model. Publishing under various pseudonyms, each year she releases more than 200 different novels, spanning the genres of romance, thriller and mystery.

Hart sees herself as an ideas person, as well as an editor and publisher. Although none of her books has yet become a bestseller, the business is profitable, she said, adding that each book reaches more than 5,000 people.

Stoffel considers the entire debate hypocritical and points out that many publishers have been working with AI tools for some time. He's certain that "right now, a million-copy bestseller is being printed that was created with the help of AI. The author won't admit it, and then there'll be a scandal."

It is entirely possible that the scandal surrounding Thelyson Orelien is precisely that story. But we may never know for sure.

For now, the battle against the tech giants continues, some of which are themselves increasingly concerned about losing control.

At the very start of the Frankfurt fair, the German Publishers and Booksellers Association issued an appeal to policymakers in Berlin and Brussels, calling for stricter regulation of artificial intelligence, which they said is more urgent than ever. More than 140 publishers have signed it.

But for now, it remains just an appeal. And the question of what authors themselves should be permitted to do with AI will undoubtedly continue to fuel debates in the future.

#1064. Newcastle fans turn on Jaissle as defeat triggers relegation concerns

Newcastle United did not just lose to Everton, they lost the home crowd, whose enthusiasm to back their team has drained from them at alarming speed.

This was a performance that belonged in the pre-takeover era, those bad old days under Steve McClaren, John Carver and Steve Bruce. It was a hugely satisfying evening for Everton manager David Moyes, who insisted there was “a way back” for Jack Grealish, even though he was once again left at home after he missed training last week without permission.

The atmosphere went flat early and gradually turned into anger and frustration. The crowd initially tried to stay with their team but were repeatedly punched in the face by the grim reality of the spectacle in front of them. They do not like the style of play, they do not like the application of the players and they cannot accept the results. They are fed up with pretending otherwise.

This was another miserable performance from Matthias Jaissle’s side, who did not manage a shot on target until the 86th minute. He has only been in the job three months, but nothing seems to be getting better.

“I have to take the responsibility,” he said. “We did not transfer the things we did in training. Hitting long balls all the time, that was not the plan. We were not brave enough to play short passes.

“As soon as the referee blew his whistle, the plan disappeared. We could feel the anger and the frustration, I felt it on the touchline. We are low on confidence and it shows.”

Newcastle looked listless, clueless and alarmingly devoid of belief in what they were being asked to do. They have the unmistakable whiff of a team in decline.

If they do not start playing a lot better, they will be worried about a relegation battle. It is four defeats in their last five games and the confidence in Jaissle to find solutions is fading. Rather than change what he is asking his team to do, he has doubled down on the formation and tactics.

Concerns have been creeping steadily upwards since August. There is a lack of confidence in the players, and worries about the quality of the eight new signings made over the summer.

In particular, there are serious misgivings about the implementation of the “vertical football” Jaissle has imported to the North East of England from the Austro-German Red Bull coaching school.

A night under the lights at St James’ Park should be a boisterous affair, but things went flat quickly. Newcastle, as they have tended to do this season, resorted to long balls punted forward. More often than not they were poorly directed – only 22 per cent were accurate over 98 minutes.

There was no fluency and no threat. The first groans were heard inside 15 minutes as another pass was hoisted harmlessly into the air. They grew more widespread and more frequent.

Everton, just as they had in their Carabao Cup win last week, looked comfortable. Recognising how easy it was to nullify Newcastle’s game plan, they offered an attacking threat of their own.

A rising shot from Merlin Röhl briefly had goalkeeper Lukas Hornicek worried. A free-kick into the Newcastle box caused panic. James Tarkowski won the first header, but Thierno Barry swung and missed with his left foot.

The groans began to turn into boos and whistles. Jaissle’s side could barely string more than two passes together. It felt precarious.

This is not an easy place to play football when the crowd airs its displeasure. As the first half limped on, there were players in black and white who looked like they could not handle the pressure.

It was a horrible game of football. With the last kick of the half, Everton should have taken the lead, Harrison Armstrong picked out Barry inside the box, but he made a mess of the finish. The referee’s whistle was accompanied by boos and a scream of “sort it out” from behind Jaissle’s technical area.

He did not follow those blunt instructions. Everton took the lead in such simple fashion and all Jaissle and his coaching staff could do was shake their heads at each other. Tyrique George was played in far too easily from a free-kick but his shot should have been saved by Hornicek. It was straight at the Czech, but it went through him and it left Barry with a tap in. Newcastle appealed for both a foul on Fabian Schar and an offside but got neither.

Newcastle tried to gain some momentum and finally created a chance. Harvey Barnes curled a cross to the far post. It bounced awkwardly but Anthony Elanga somehow failed to bundle it across the line.

We take it game by game but tonight feels good and we can look forward to Friday [against Coventry].”

Thierno Barry puts Everton ahead after Tyrique George's shot isn't dealt with by Lukáš Horníček! 🔵 https://t.co/oRXsrwbOhz

The weather in the north east has certainly taken a turn for the worse with the rain hammering down.

We are back under way at St James’ Park as the rain begins to fall. You would assume that Newcastle will not be as poor in this second half as they were in the first. Will Everton live to regret not taking a few good chances in that first half?

“They [Newcastle] have been poor, and the supporters have let them know how poor they have been. Everton have been far the better side. David Moyes will be pleased but disappointed that they are not 1-0 in front.”

Armstrong should probably put Everton in front with the last kick of the half but misses the target. Dewsbury-Hall cuts the ball back from the left to pick out the run of Armstrong into the penalty area. From the penalty spot, Armstrong opens up his right foot to try and guide it into the far corner but his effort goes just wide.

That is the final act of the half and it remains goalless at St James’ Park. Some boos ring around the stadium as the players head off.

That is a good late chance in the half for Everton. Dewsbury-Hall clips a dangerous ball in from the left and picks out O’Brien at the back post but the defender cannot guide his header on target. That was whilst Hall was still off and Barnes was operating as a temporary left-back.

Hall has received some treatment to his back and is now back to his feet.

Hall has stayed down after Barry collided into the back of the Newcastle left-back going up for a header.

George is dispossessed inside his own half before Willock plays it forward to Joelinton. The Brazilian takes one touch before shooting from just outside the box but his effort flies wide of Pickford’s left post. Joelinton struck it powerfully but cut cross the ball too much.

Barnes cuts inside from the left and drives across the face of the penalty area. His shot is semi-blocked by Branthwaite and loops into the air towards his own goal. Pickford takes no risks and palms it over his own bar. Hall’s delivery is headed on by Burn but then cleared by Mykolenko.

Garner is the one to take it but his effort is blocked by the wall. He tried to beat Hornicek at his near post rather than go completely over the wall but the end of the wall still blocks it.

Barry is fouled by Burn just outside the Newcastle penalty area and the latter is the first player into the book tonight. Burn protests his innocence but replays show that the referee was 100% correct with his decision. Burn is a touch fortunate that it is just outside the box. Garner and Dewsbury-Hall are stood over this one...

I would say that the Newcastle fans have gone from frustrated to now quite annoyed with how their side has begun this game. Plenty of groans and moans inside St James’ Park; their only relief will be that they are not behind.

David Moyes will be desperate to see his side score and take advantage of Newcastle not being at the races. The frustration from the home fans continues to grow and this is Everton’s opportunity. You cannot imagine that Newcastle will be this poor throughout the game.

That is a glorious chance for Barry that he should really have taken. A free-kick is sent into the Newcastle box and Branthwaite wins the header. The ball falls to Barry who, from ten yards out, has a big chance to put Everton in front but instead it is more of an air shot. In fact, he ends up kicking Osula to gift Newcastle a free-kick.

Rohl has Everton’s first proper sighting of goal tonight but he wastes the opportunity from the right side of the box, failing to keep his shot down and sees it go over Hornicek’s bar.

We are seeing many of the same issues with Newcastle United’s so-called vertical football under Matthias Jaissle already this evening.

Aimless long balls to nobody hoisted forward. Long balls aimed at someone who fails to win the first header or challenge and possession is given back to Everton.

There have already been a few grumbles from the home crowd as William Osula is sent off on another forlorn chase of an over-hit pass in behind the Everton centre backs.

We are nearly 20 minutes into the game and Everton striker Barry is still yet to touch the ball.

Joelinton’s shot from the edge of the box is struck powerfully and is blocked by Tarkowski, going behind for Newcastle’s first corner of the night. Hall’s delivery beyond the back post finds Burn but his header from just a few yards out goes wide. Burn should really be hitting the target from so close to the goal.

We are just a quarter of an hour into this one but you can already sense some frustration from the home fans. Everton, despite being away from home, have settled well into this game.

To sum up the frustration from the home supporters, Dedic plays a dreadful long free-kick into the box that has far too much on it and goes behind.

Under the lights at home, you would assume Matthias Jaissle would have wanted a fast start from his side but that has not happened for the hosts.

Barnes is afforded space to cut inside from the left and, from the corner of the penalty area, clips a dangerous ball towards the far post. There is slightly too much on it and the ball goes behind for a goal-kick, although for a moment Pickford appeared to be panicking. That is the second time Barnes has been given too much space to cut inside and if Everton keep allowing that, you would imagine that they will eventually be punished.

The two starting XIs are fairly similar to the ones that started on Thursday night but the obvious difference between the League Cup tie and tonight’s Premier League encounter is the change of ground. How big an impact can the Newcastle fans have on the outcome of this one?

Unsurprisingly, former Sunderland goalkeeper Pickford is roundly booed by the home crowd upon his first touch.

Ahead of Remembrance Sunday this coming weekend, with this being Newcastle’s final home league game before then, St James’ Park pauses to remember all those who have given their lives to protect this country. The Last Post is played after St James’ Park falls silent.

Both sides emerge from the tunnel and we are just moments away from kick-off from St James’ Park. Here is a reminder of how the sides line up this evening:

Newcastle: Hornicek; Dedic, Schar, Burn, Hall; Joelinton, Gonzalez; Elanga, Willock, Barnes; Osula.Substitutes: Pope, Botman, Bamba, Wissa, Thiaw, Steur, Toure, Murphy, Ramsey.

“I think everybody who has been in football and comes to St James’ Park knows what the atmosphere is like here. We have to try and quell it the best way we can. Newcastle have got some really good players. It is a Premier League game, we know a lot about them, they know a lot about us. I do not think there are too many big surprises tonight.”

“We picked up on what we can do better [against Everton], this is something we focused on in training, really committed in the last few days so hopefully we can deliver today.”

On Anthony Elanga returning to the starting line-up:

“It is important now after he was out for a long time with an injury. Now he is improving a lot physically and also getting the feeling to play with the lads again. Therefore he deserves to start today and hopefully he can put his potential on the pitch.”

On Will Osula starting after an injury scare:

“He is such a talented guy, young lad, he can cause any opposition problems so hopefully he can deliver that again with his strength.”

On what he is hoping for tonight to get the three points:

“Be clinical, ruthless in both boxes. Defend with everything you have and then be efficient and use every opportunity to score and then I think we will see a great result today.”

“That helps us for sure. The extra motivation and extra energy will be there from the stands and that is something that we can always count on here at home in our stadium.”

“Nothing more than what I am sure you have already heard so he is not in the team tonight.”

This was going to be a younger, more dynamic squad that would grow with the club as they looked to live up to the promise made by David Hopkinson, the chief executive, that they would be “consistently and credibly challenging” for top honours in England and Europe by 2030.

Having sold Bruno Guimarães (£73m), Sandro Tonali (£90m) and Anthony Gordon (£67m), Newcastle were able to spend roughly £262.9m on eight players to reinvigorate the squad as they once again talked about challenging for European qualification in Matthias Jaissle’s first season as manager.

Newcastle are 12th in the Premier League, but have had an inconsistent start and there are concerns that too many of these signings have failed to shine. Jaissle is leaning heavily on the players he inherited from Howe instead.

It is always worth remembering that you only get a true reading of the Premier League table after ten games so this is a pivotal moment for both Newcastle and Everton as they play their ninth match of the campaign.

For Newcastle, a win tonight would take them up to seventh, just two points behind Chelsea in fourth. Despite the heavy away defeats and unconvincing performances, that would be an impressive start for a new manager. Matthias Jaissle has already felt the full force of the contrasting emotions on Tyneside in his three months in charge but big questions hang over his team. In particular, the “vertical football” style he brought from the Red Bull coaching school in Germany.

A defeat tonight, coming so soon after the 3-1 defeat in the Carabao Cup to Everton, will intensify the criticism of his approach.  It would also suggest Newcastle, despite all their positive talk over the summer, are nothing more than a mid-table team who will be looking over their shoulders rather than upwards this season.

A win for Everton will have the same uplift for David Moyes at Everton, also taking them up to seventh in the table. Given all the problems attached to their summer recruitment - or rather the lack of it - Everton will have defied the grim pre-season predictions heading into the second international break. The table is starting to take shape and so are the narratives around every club.
