#1049. Pope lung nodule: Could it be cancer?

The case of Pope Leo shows how small lung nodules are often found during routine health checks. Quick treatment is generally advised before nodules can grow to become larger life-threatening masses.

It often takes a chest X-ray or CT scan to spot small lung (or pulmonary) nodules, especially when a patient is asymptomatic.

At less than 3 centimeters (1.1 inches), lung nodules are less likely to press against your airway and cause any chest pain or shortness of breath or wheezing.

In the case of Pope Leo XIV, who told a gathering at the Vatican on October 11, 2026, doctors had found a nodule on his lung, it is unclear exactly how large that nodule is.

All we know (at time of writing on October 12, 2026) is that it was "detected at a very early stage," and that it was "well localized."

That suggests it has not spread or metastasized, although its full status is not publicly known. Doctors advised the pontiff to have his lung nodule removed.

Whether his was a chance finding — or whether the pope had presented with symptoms — we do not know.

But "incidental findings of lung nodule(s) in asymptomatic individuals" is considered an "increasingly common clinical dilemma," according to a 2019 paper published in the Annals of Thoracic Medicine.

This "dilemma" rests in part on the fact that biopsies — removing a small sample of tissue from the spot or nodule to determine whether it's malignant (cancerous) — are difficult to perform on small nodules.

The risks involved in a surgical diagnosis are considered "excessive compared to the relatively low prevalence of malignancy in the small nodules."

That's according to a 2017 paper published in the European Respiratory Review. And that may also be the dilemma that Pope Leo's doctors have faced.

Fortunately many — if not most — early-stage lung nodules are benign. It is also possible to have more than one nodule at a time, and they can all be benign.

It's said the pope will need a week to recover after his operation to remove the lung nodule. He is due to travel to Uruguay, Argentina and Peru between November 6-17.

Lung nodules are generally defined as a white spot or lesion on the lung. They have a rounded or irregular shape.

Radiologists refer to their "opacity" because, compared to the surrounding air-filled lung tissue, lung nodules appear as white or gray spots on a CT scan — that is, they have a certain density.

Lung nodules can be caused by old lung infections, foreign particles that are inhaled and get lodged in the lung, inflammation, scar tissue and indeed the onset of cancer.

At more than 3 centimeters, the nodule is defined as a mass. The bigger it gets, the greater the chance that it will obstruct your airway and the lung's ability to function.

Symptoms may start with chest pain, shortness of breath and wheezing. They may then progress to a chronic cough or coughing up of blood, fatigue, hoarseness, loss of appetite, unexplained weight loss and recurring respiratory infections like bronchitis or pneumonia.

It is hard to determine when lung nodules become life-threatening cancer. But one indicator of a lung nodule's malignancy is its size.

At 2 milimeters or smaller, the risk of cancer is very small and remains so up to a nodule size of about 6-7 milimeters.

The risk of cancer becomes 9%-10% at about 8 to 10 milimeters. And at larger than 1 centimeter, the risk of cancer is about 15%.

The density of a lung nodule is also a vital indicator of malignancy.

There are two main categories of lung nodule density: solid and subsolid. Subsolid nodules are further divided into pure ground-glass (nonsolid) and part-solid nodules.

According to a 2026 review article published in the New England Journal of Medicine, subsolid nodules are less prevalent than solid nodules, but they have "a higher likelihood of being malignant."

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

It is said that radiologists see lung nodules in about 30% of chest CT scans. But that number may be rising.

A Dutch study published in 2023 cited an increase in lung nodule detections from 38% of scans in 2008 to 50% in 2019. The same study said "the proportion of patients in whom significant new nodules (≥ 5 mm) were reported increased from 9% in 2010 to 17% in 2017."

However, this may also be a result of the development of better scanning technology in recent years and the use of artificial intelligence to spot tumors.

Bearing in mind that most lung nodules are benign, lung cancer does tend to start with a lesion or nodule. And lung cancer remains the most common type of cancer and the most common cause of cancer death in the world.

The World Health Organization's International Agency for Research on Cancer says that in 2024 almost 2.65 million people were diagnosed with lung cancer and more than 1.8 million people died from the disease.

With a stylish assist and a gorgeous goal, Viktor Gyokeres produced the sort of match-winning performance that suggests the Swedish striker is making significant progress at last. It has not always been straightforward for him at Arsenal, but this was unquestionably one of his better showings, and it continued an encouraging upturn in his form.

Gyokeres has been the second-choice striker for most of this season, with Mikel Arteta usually preferring the more subtle Kai Havertz in attack. There are signs, though, that Gyokeres is now growing in belief. Following this victory over Slavia Prague, which was much more narrow and nervy than it should have been, he has now scored two goals and registered three assists in his last five appearances.

Even more promising than those statistics was his all-round play in Prague. In the first half especially, Gyokeres held on to long passes, combined with his team-mates and tested the opposition with his runs in behind. For Arsenal’s first goal, he found Noni Madueke with a brilliant pass. For their second, he curled a fabulous strike into the top corner.

“Really good,” said Arteta of Gyokeres. “Not only the assist and the goal, but he was really connected to the team. It’s great news, because I think he needed that performance.”

Those two moments in the first half eventually ensured another European victory for Arteta’s side, but the manager was far from impressed with the second-half showing. So smooth at first, Arsenal became remarkably ragged by the end. Slavia were deserving of their goal, scored by Wiktor Nowak. It looked like complacency had infected the minds of the Arsenal players, and you could feel Arteta’s fury radiating from the touchline.

“We scored two goals and it should have been three, four or five,” said Arteta. “And at half-time the message was clear: there is still a lot to do in this game. Right from the beginning of the second half, we were extremely far from our standards in everything that we have to do, in every basic, in every concept, and in everything we discussed. So much to improve and I take full responsibility for that.”

Without Gabriel Magalhães and David Raya, who both made dramatic stops on the goal-line, this could have become an ugly night for Arsenal against one of the weaker teams in the Champions League. The Czech side have now gone 23 games without a victory in Europe’s premier competition, which equals the longest winless run in European Cup history.

It was a remarkable coincidence that this game fell on November 4, the exact date as the same fixture last season. On that occasion Arsenal were comfortable 3-0 winners, with Mikel Merino scoring twice, and they seemed to be heading towards a similar night when Madueke scored the early opener.

The goal was made by Gyokeres, who held off a defender and then hooked an excellent pass into Madueke’s path. The Arsenal winger had already established his dominance over Oskar Kubiak, his opposite number, and he reached fifth gear before the Polish defender had even reached second. Madueke then slid his finish beneath the body of Nazar Domchak, Slavia’s teenage goalkeeper.

Just as Gyokeres is finding his form, so is Madueke. The absence of the injured Bukayo Saka has given Madueke a run in the side and he seems to be benefiting from it, even if he still lacks the same consistency in decision-making as his England team-mate.

One of Slavia’s many problems in a one-sided first half was their inability to cope with Arsenal’s rotations in midfield. Declan Rice, Martín Zubimendi and Merino were all alternating positions at will, taking turns to drop deep and push forward. Gyokeres has never been the most delicate link-up player, and there have been too many times when the ball has simply bounced off him, but here he was impressively sleek. A quick exchange of passes with Merino allowed him a sight of goal, and the curled finish was sumptuous. For a man known for his power, this was an uncharacteristic demonstration of finesse.

Game over? Arsenal clearly thought so. They certainly came out for the second half like a team that believed the job was done. Arsenal return to Slavia Prague for the third time under Mikel Arteta knowing that three points will be another step towards a top-eight finish in the Champions League league phase.

Arteta’s team were 4-0 winners in the Czech capital in a 2021 Europa League quarter-final second leg, and 3-0 victors at this stage of the Champions League a year ago. Bukayo Saka opened the scoring with a penalty before two second-half goals from Mikel Merino.

Slavia Prague are top of the Czech league and unbeaten after 13 games this season, but they are winless in the Champions League after fixtures against Lens, Sabah and Fernerbahce.

The fixture should be a presentable opportunity for Arteta to rotate his team, especially after a physically taxing game at Anfield where Arsenal showed their mettle to win at Liverpool’s home for the first time since 2012.

Arsenal’s second-string is very strong, though they did not cover themselves in glory at Fleetwood in the League Cup last week when Max Dowman was sent off. Given the 16-year-old is banned for another two Premier League games, and the attention Arteta’s touchline reaction to the red card attracted, one wonders if he might want to seize a chance to put Dowman back on the horse.

William Saliba’s return to full training is very welcome news, despite Ezri Konsa impressing in his absence. Saliba travelled with the squad to Prague, and could make his first appearance of the season following a back injury which flared up in France’s World Cup semi-final against Spain. With fixtures against Manchester City, Borussia Dortmund, Brentford, Spurs, Real Madrid, Bournemouth and Manchester United before the end of 2026 though, they will not want rush him.

Piero Hincapie, Cristhian Mosquera, Martin Zubimendi, Merino, Viktor Gyokeres and Eberechi Eze are other players pushing for greater involvement from the start of matches.

#1047. Rise of Germanic and Celtic languages is written in ancient DNA

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Aghascrebagh Ogham Stone in Northern Ireland shows much-worn inscriptions.Credit: Radharc Images/Alamy

More than one billion people worldwide speak Germanic languages such as English, German and Dutch, whereas Celtic languages — including Welsh, Irish and Gaelic — are spoken by only two or three million people, mostly in northern Europe.

A pair of studies analysing more than 4,700 ancient human genomes has now identified the possible origins of Celtic1 and Germanic2 languages and found migrations that might have dispersed their speakers around Europe — partly explaining their distribution today. The papers were published in Nature on 4 November.

Linguistic and archaeological studies have indicated that Celtic languages were widespread across Europe about 2,500 years ago, reaching into present-day Italy, Spain and France. Speakers of early Germanic languages might have been limited to a pocket of northern Germany, Scandinavia and the Baltic Sea coast some 3,000 years ago.

“We wanted to kind of see how this change occurs. How does the range swap through time?” says Hugh McColl, a population geneticist at the University of Copenhagen and a co-author of both studies.

How one language family took over the world: ancient DNA traces its spread

How one language family took over the world: ancient DNA traces its spread

Linguists have previously proposed that migrations played some part in the dispersal of Germanic and Celtic languages. But Guus Kroonen, a historical linguist at Leiden University in the Netherlands and a co-author of both studies, says that there are other ways for languages to spread. “You can easily adopt a new language without changing your genes.”

McColl, Kroonen and their colleagues looked for signs of migration through shifts in the ancestry of ancient population groups. To do so, they used newly sequenced genomes from more than 700 people, alongside published data from some 4,000 ancient humans.

The researchers identified an enigmatic population that migrated to Sweden around 4,000 years ago, possibly from Baltic regions. They found that the presence of this ancestry in Scandinavia and its spread throughout Europe was consistent with previous linguistic theories and archaeological evidence. “It’s a good tracer dye for the spread of Germanic languages,” says Kroonen.

For instance, the ancestry was present in southern Scandinavia and northern Germany around 3,000 years ago, when linguistic evidence points to exchanges with other language groups in this region. After some 1,000 years, the population moved into central, southern and western Europe, including the British Isles, which also chimes with linguists’ ideas and historical evidence about the spread of these languages, such as the first appearance of Germanic language inscriptions, called runes, around 2,000 years ago. The ancestry was present in Anglo-Saxon individuals in Britain, who spoke a Germanic precursor to Old English.

The study on the spread of Germanic languages also turned up a surprising ‘back-migration’ of people from present-day Germany into Scandinavia, which coincided with the emergence of Old Norse — the predecessor of modern Scandinavian languages — and with the Vikings’ influence on the region.

The Rök Stone, which bears the longest runic carving on stone with more than 700 characters, is thought to have been erected by Vikings in present-day Östergötland, Sweden.Credit: JEPPE GUSTAFSSON/TT News Agency/AFP via Getty

In many cases, the expansion of Germanic languages occurred in regions where Celtic languages were dominant.

Linguists debate both where Celtic languages emerged and how they became so widespread, says McColl, with some favouring an Atlantic origin overlapping with the current range of Celtic speakers in the British Isles. Other models put Celtic origins farther east, in Europe.

#1046. Why were Leeds not given a penalty for handball against Mateus Fernandes?

Please refresh the page or navigate to another page on the site to be automatically logged inPlease refresh your browser to be logged in

Fernandes dove across with his arm fully extended to get in front of a Gabriel Gudmundsson’s cross

Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.

Mateus Fernandes was fortunate to come away from an early penalty call unscathed in Tottenham’s Premier League clash with Leeds after his out-stretched arm blocked a cross in the box.

Gabriel Gudmundsson whipped in the ball from the left flank aiming for Dominic Calvert-Lewin in the fourth minute, with Spurs midfielder Fernandes diving across with his arm fully extended to get in the way.

The ball appeared to bounce off either the top of his arm or his shoulder, with Leeds players vocally appealing for a penalty along with the Elland Road faithful.

Initial replays failed to give a definitive answer on which part of his body the ball hit, with the TNT Sports commentary team - made up of Steven Gerrard, Lucy Ward and commentator Darren Fletcher - stressing that the decision was anything but cut and dry.

“It’s extremely close. He’s got away with one, I think,” said Gerrard.

“It doesn’t look like the chest to me. If anything it hits the shoulder and the top of the arm. In slow motion it looks worse.”

VAR reviewed the incident, telling referee John Brooks to briefly halt play after the ball went out.

And while VAR confirmed that the ball did hit Fernandes’ arm, Brooks was ultimately not advised to award a spot kick.

“The referee’s call of no penalty to Leeds United was checked and confirmed by VAR – with it deemed that Fernandes did not commit a handball offence,” the Premier League Match Centre said.

Quoting VAR, the statement added: “Confirming the on-field decision of play on. The ball strikes the very top of the arm as he is leaning – in the green zone.”

As per refereeing body Ifab’s rules, the “green zone” for handball is the very top of the shoulder and the upper sleeve area, with contact here being legal. Anything further down the arm is classified as handball.

#1044. 125 years of Thomas Mann's 'Buddenbrooks'

This over 1,000-page masterpiece offers a panoramic view of society in the 19th century and exposes the collapse of a merchant family: unrecognized sons, disillusioned daughters and the loss of middle-class ideals.

Who would have imagined it in the beginning? A 26-year-old man without a high school diploma, but greatly ambitious, writes a two-pound book with a melancholy undertone. "I'm not exactly delighted," his publisher initially responded. But he ended up publishing the novel anyway, more out of goodwill than conviction. And the rest is history.

For many, Thomas Mann's Buddenbrooks is considered THE German social novel. It is indeed a classic, and one that garnered the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1929. Global fame, an international best-seller, and required reading for many German students. Anyone who mentions Thomas Mann thinks of Buddenbrooks in the same breath. Why is that?

Does the explanation lie in the autobiographical connections between the work and the author?

Thomas Mann was born in Lübeck to a merchant family, but his artistic aspirations did not fit in well in the middle-class mainstream. This struggle inspired Mann's first work. The inability of this sensitive bohemian to carry on the family's time-honored business after the death of his father was sniffed at and derided.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Reflecting the situation of his novel's character Hanno, Mann had a privileged life in a wealthy family, but one that was at risk of collapse. The aspiring novelist also had to withstand disappointing the expectations of others. He was forced to defend his dream of an artistic life. Yet as much as he was inspired by real life, he forcefully altered these biographical details to place his unique literary mark on his writing.

But does that really matter in light of people who choose not to make the distinction between an author's life and his work? Even though the name "Lübeck" does not appear in the novel, citizens there felt markedly insulted after the publication of Buddenbrooks in 1901.

That likely lies in the fact that the image the author portrayed was not one of an idyllic northern German city, but one of a place that had difficulty blending tradition with modernity.

This contradiction is also seen in each of the figures in the novel. Nothing is like it appears. Mann lays down this foundation of this skepticism from the very beginning, in a scene taking place on a very ordinary Thursday in October 1835. The Buddenbrook family comes together for their ordinary late lunch.

"There they all sat, on heavy, high-backed chairs, consuming good heavy food from good silver plates, drinking full-bodied wines and expressing their views freely on all subjects. When they began to talk shop, they slipped unconsciously more and more into dialect, and used the clumsy but comfortable idioms that seemed to embody to them the business efficiency and the easy well-being of their community. Sometimes they even used an over-drawn pronunciation by way of making fun of themselves and each other, and relished their clipped phrases and exaggerated vowels with the same heartiness they did their food."

There sits the leader of the family company, Johann Buddenbrook the Elder, and his wife, his son and counsel Jean, along with his family. The grandchildren are also there: Tony the dreamer, the quarrelsome rebel Christian, and Thomas, the eldest grandchild.

It is Thomas who is supposed to later take on the responsibility of continuing the family tradition, regardless of the cost. Mann weaves his narrative work starting with this main family, and then across several generations.

But appearances in the family are deceptive. The reader senses it's all headed toward a downfall. The new house is taken over from a family that was once as illustrious as the Buddenbrooks, but faced financial ruin and had to leave.

Johann and his family aim to make a better go of it. They make decisions on what is demanded economically, but fail — financially, interpersonally, and mentally.

Tony and Thomas end up falling in love with people not befitting their social standing, but do not have the courage to stand up to their parents. They enter marriages of convenience, yet it is these partnerships that paradoxically set disaster in motion.

From an early age, Thomas Mann was influenced by Schopenhauer's pessimistic notion of the will being a blind force at work in the world. Thus, there is likewise no escape for the Buddenbrooks. They speak of emotions and morality, yet it is money and economics that steer the ship. Failure, decline and even death seem to be the only viable outcome.

Mann also punctuates this hopelessness in a stylistic manner, by consistently repeating entire passages word for word, or evoking motifs such as the family registry or the estate in all their various forms.

The extent of this demise appears linguistically molded and exaggerated. The Buddenbrooks, this proud north German family of refinement, actually speaks the vernacular studded with empty French expressions. "Je, den Düwel ook, c'est la question, ma très chère demoiselle!"

The lowly servants, the courtesans, and the demi-monde: all of them speak the language of the street, raw and unpolished. In a virtuoso manner, Thomas Mann orchestrated this mass of voices into a panorama of society in the 19th century. The snobbishness on the part of the Buddenbrooks thus appears as a relic of a long lost time. It's a symbol of their inability to adapt to change and place their faith in progress.

Yet the fact that this extensive work spanning several generations does not get weighed down by aesthetic excess is purely due to Mann's brilliance as an author. He is able to bring every one of his numerous characters to life in words. Life that is full of complexity, contradictions and ambiguities. Some of these characters accompany the reader page for page; others appear only briefly.

And yet one begins to contemplate how someone like Grünlich could become a dodgy, unscrupulous husband and catches oneself wanting to chase the fearful Hanno out of the music conservatory and yell to him: "Go, throw yourself into life! You are not a failure." It is precisely this empathy that spurs one on to read through the night and prompts one to chuckle at all the intricate sentences and philosophical digressions.

Thomas Mann: Buddenbrooks, Vintage Classics / Penguin Random House, (German title: Buddenbrooks, 1901). English translation: John E. Woods

Thomas Mann was born into a privileged Lübeck merchant family in 1875. He died in Zurich, Switzerland in 1955. "I am a townsman, a citizen, a child and a great-grandchild of German bourgeois society," the author once wrote about himself. Mann received the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1929 for his debut novel, Buddenbrooks. He also garnered numerous other prizes and honors for his extensive work, including Death in Venice (1911), The Magic Mountain (1924), and the tetralogy Joseph and His Brothers (1933-1943). He emigrated to Switzerland in 1933, and to the US in 1938. From there, he made his famous radio commentaries in which he agitated against the Nazis. He returned to Switzerland in 1952.

This article was first published as part of the series 100 German must-reads.

#1043. Fulham end winless run with first league victory for under-pressure Alvaro Arbeloa

Please refresh the page or navigate to another page on the site to be automatically logged inPlease refresh your browser to be logged in

Fulham 1-0 Hull City: Alex Iwobi’s first-half goal gave the Cottagers their first league win of the season

Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.

Fulham’s winless run under Alvaro Arbeloa was finally ended by an entertaining 1-0 victory over Hull at Craven Cottage.

Alex Iwobi struck the winner in the 33rd minute to lift the home side off the foot of the Premier League table and out of the bottom three, though goalkeeper Konstantinos Tzolakis will wonder how he ever let the shot spill through him.

It meant valuable breathing room for Arbeloa whose position had come under scrutiny after failing to win any of his first six league matches in charge, though a red card in the final seconds for Ryan Sessegnon for leaving his studs on Robinio Vaz marred the afternoon.

Fulham had dropped eight points from winning positions this season, including five when they had led inside the final two minutes, and their wastefulness after going in front was alarming, if not ultimately costly.

Gonzalo Garcia in particular spurned a golden opportunity when he headed against the crossbar with the six-yard box to himself. It was the kind of chance the former Real Madrid striker was brought in to bury, and Fulham may yet find their position remains perilous if they continue to give up chances like this.

Hull were a pale impression of the team that had begun the season with such attacking ambition, and the passiveness with which they approached a game against the side propping up the league will have been of concern for Sergej Jakirovic.

Fulham dominated from the start and went close when Iwobi’s shot was deflected on to the roof of the net in the third minute.

The hosts were playing like a team desperate for a win, with Oscar Bobb and Timothy Castagne in particular menacing Hull down their left.

The breakthrough came just after the half hour. Brooke Norton-Cuffy’s clearance was poor and from there Hull never recovered.

Sander Berge took possession and knocked it back to the edge of the box for Iwobi, whose driven finish squirmed through the body of Tzolakis. The goalkeeper could point to a slight deflection, but it was a poor error.

In the second half, Tzolakis partially redeemed himself with a good save with his feet to deny Josh King, after Semi Ajayi had played his team into a mess with an awful pass out of defence.

Fulham were beginning to show what they were capable of. King’s touch on the hour to spin away from Ajayi was a delight. The 19-year-old then drove forward and crossed for Garcia to head into the path of Iwobi, and only a magnificent save from Tzolakis denied the Cottagers what would have surely been one of the goals of the season.

Iwobi came close again with a curling effort that dropped just wide of the near post.

Hull were clinging on, but all the while the spectre of dropped points hung over Fulham as long as the second goal eluded them.

Nervousness around the ground intensified after Garcia planted a free header against the crossbar from six yards.

But they held on despite Sessegnon, on as a late substitute, being dismissed with virtually the last action, though there was clearly no violent intent behind his challenge on Vaz.

#1042. Tuchel: Bellingham and I were up and down – now we are in a good place

England head coach Thomas Tuchel described his relationship with Jude Bellingham as being “in a good place” after admitting it had been “a bit up and down”.

Tuchel has two Bellinghams in his latest England squad after calling up Jude’s brother, Jobe, for the first time for the Nations League games against Croatia and Spain. If they play together, it will be the first time brothers have represented England in the same team since Gary and Phil Neville 19 years ago.

This time last year, Tuchel cast doubt over Jude’s place in his team by picking Morgan Rogers over him, having not included the Real Madrid midfielder in an England squad the previous month.

But Jude performed superbly for Tuchel at the World Cup and was England’s best player during the last international camp. Tuchel revealed he has listened to his advice by calling up 21-year-old Jobe.

Asked if his relationship with Jude has developed, Tuchel said: “It was a bit of an up and down [relationship] of course, but we are in a good place.

“I love to be his coach, he’s a top player, a very influential player and it goes both ways. If Jude was not feeling comfortable, he would not perform at that level.

“At the moment, you see he’s happy to come into camp, he’s happy with the role he has, he’s fully invested and now to have the chance to have both of them [Bellingham brothers] is just the next step. I hope we have finished with the down. You never know as a coach.”

Jobe has captained England’s Under-21s and, as well as U21 head coach Lee Carlsey, Tuchel acknowledged the influence of Jude on the Borussia Dortmund midfielder’s first senior call.

Jude once said that playing with Jobe for England would be “the biggest dream of my life” and that it would mean more to him than any trophies.

Discussing Jude’s influence on Jobe’s selection, Tuchel said: “We spoke about his brother because I was aware it was always his dream and Jude was always like, ‘Watch him, he’s good, he can make it,’ I would say, ‘Yeah we are watching him.’ And we know, of course, from Lee Carsley and we see him with the Under-21s and there is such positive feedback.

“This is also the signal that if you are good in the Under-21s, this is the next step. We had it with Elliot Anderson, we had it with Alex Scott, we have it with Jarell Quansah and it counts. If you play good for England in the Under-19s, 20s, 21s, if you play good for England in tournaments then it means something.”

Tuchel at one point had to correct himself, with a laugh, when he accidentally referred to Jobe as Jube. On the subject of how Jobe reacted to his call-up and the comparisons with his brother that he will inevitably face, Tuchel said: “He has to live with this that everyone will compare them. They look similar, even in their movements, but they are very different players. And let’s see – they are also different characters, at least that’s what I heard.

“He [Jobe] watched training very early in my [reign]. In my first March camp maybe, he came over and watched his brother train. We chatted and we said, ‘Ah, it would be nice if one day you are with him [Jude].’ He was very kind and polite and I’m glad to have him in camp.

“He couldn’t stop smiling [when I told him]. He has the same beautiful smile as Jude, so it’s nice to have him. Let’s see what the effect is. What I saw, Jude was always the big brother that you imagine, taking care of his younger brother and making sure everything is alright. Behaving like a big brother. And that helps Jobe now. And it will be beautiful for Jude to have his brother close and in camp and to have this experience together. It’s a very special moment for them.”

Lee Carsley has been talking highly about Jobe for weeks and months, that he deserves it if there is a spot and a possibility to join and to make an impression in the first team.

He had good matches and is on a good run of form with Dortmund so he deserves to be with us. We have 21 outfield players for the first match and then possibly 22 for the second match. [Lewis-Skelly is suspended for the Croatia match after picking up two bookings in the opening games].

Thomas Tuchel has Jordan Henderson back fit – and playing well – since the last international break. The last of Henderson’s 91 caps came at the World Cup against Panama, with his tournament effectively ended when he famously broke his arm in the celebrations at the Azteca after Mexico were defeated. From Tuchel’s squad in the summer, Djed Spence has also returned from injury although he is only just back playing for Inter Milan.

Marcus Rashford is set to miss out on England through injury having barely played since the last international break. The Manchester United forward pulled out of the last squad, then returned for his club the following weekend. But he has not featured since the defeat to Atletico Madrid in the Champions League. His absence will open up a space for another wide forward, with Noni Madueke pushing for a call-up with his form for Arsenal.

Good morning and welcome to live coverage of the announcement by Thomas Tuchel of England’s squad for their remaining two Uefa Nations Group 3 matches against Croatia – them again – at Wembley next Thursday and Spain at the Metropolitano in Madrid next Sunday night. England have already qualified for the knockout phase – barring a defeat by Croatia by a margin of eight or more goals – but would need two victories to avoid France and Portugal in the next two-legged phase in March.

Tuchel’s only major injury doubt from the last squad are Arsenal’s Bukao Saka and Como’s Trevoh Chalobah as well as the more long-term absentee Tino Livramento, the man Chalobah replaced in the World Cup 26. Djed Spence has returned to full fitness and played for Inter in their Milan derby defeat last weekend while the head coach’s favourite player, Jordan Henderson, has been passed fit to play for Chelsea at his boyhood club Sunderland on Sunday though at 36 his race may finally have been run at this level despite his unexpected encore in the last 18 months.

For the first time since 2001 England will have the Ballon d’Or winner in the squad and Harry Kane will also become England’s most-capped player – barring some misfortune when Bayern Munich take on Mainz on Saturday – by leading them out at Wembley on Thursday night for his 126th appearance.

Whether he will be joined by Cole Palmer in the squad remains the only significant issue of note. The Chelsea forward pulled out of the last squad as part of his club’s management of his groin injury but he has played in their last four Premier League games, scoring once and being sent off once as well. Kobbie Mainoo is fit again and may be picked to see if his backside has recovered from bench splinters since his summer of exasperation.

The squad will be released at 10am and followed by Tuchel’s explanations, which we will also cover here, an hour later.

#1041. Germany's China calculation shifts as import pressures eclipse export benefits

Germany has long resisted tougher action against China, fearing retaliation. But rising pressure on key industries has pushed Berlin to seek stronger EU trade-defense powers to protect its industrial base.

Germany's cautious approach toward Beijing is cracking. For years, Berlin blocked a harder line on what the European Union describes as China's  unfair trade practices.

In the last few months, that caution — a fear of Chinese retaliation that could hurt German exporters — has given way to a willingness to escalate.

Last week, Chancellor Friedrich Merz and French President Emmanuel Macron wrote jointly to European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen seeking a new tool to cut a trading partner off from the EU's single market if unfair practices continue.

Clearly aimed at Beijing, the letter warned the measure was necessary against countries that "deliberately seek to undermine ... fair market conditions by political or economic means."

China's Commerce Ministry warned Europe would "suffer the consequences" if it adopted such a "kill-switch" plan, which was timed to coincide with crucial EU-China trade talks in Beijing last week.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Noah Barkin, a senior adviser with research consultancy Rhodium Group's China practice, told DW that the threats to Germany's export powerhouse "have convinced Merz and his closest advisers that the benefits of action outweigh the costs of inaction."

Before the COVID pandemic, the two economies rose in tandem and German industry benefited from China's ascent.

Since 2021, however, China has fallen from Germany's second-largest export market to its ninth, according to data from Germany Trade & Invest for the first half of 2026.

Chinese competitors have quickly closed the technology gap and benefit from much lower costs and state subsidies. That pressure is being felt especially in Germany's automaking, precision engineering and chemicals industries.

German vehicle makers have suffered a large sales drop in China, which was once their second-largest market. According to data from Rhodium Group, German car exports to China plummeted by 66% between 2022 and 2025.

Big German brands now face heavy rivalry from a new wave of Chinese electric vehicle (EV) manufactures in other major markets, including Europe, which is forcing a wave of layoffs and possible factory closures.

In Germany alone, imports of new Chinese-made cars rose 121% in the first seven months of the year, according to Destatis, the federal statistics agency. Overall, Chinese-made vehicles accounted for nearly 14% of total vehicle imports.

"After continuously losing market share in China ... it [the rivalry] seems to be hitting their business within the European automotive market," Andreas Mischer, an associate fellow at the Berlin-based Mercator Institute for China Studies (MERICS), told DW.

Mischer said pressure from Germany's powerful automotive lobby was key to Berlin's "shifting attitude toward trade defense instruments."

Among the many German business leaders who have demanded a more hard-line approach in recent months, Oliver Richtberg, head of foreign trade at VDMA, Germany's mechanical engineering association, was perhaps the most blunt:

"We are currently being deindustrialized through unfair measures — and most companies are no longer willing to accept this," Richtberg told Welt am Sonntag newspaper in August.

According to Eurostat, the wider EU's goods deficit with China was around €360 billion ($402 billion) last year — effectively €1 billion per day — and widened again in the first half of 2026.

While Brussels has been pushing back against the dumping of cheap Chinese goods, a separate industrial protection law and other anti-coercion measures are running into trouble from Beijing and at home.

The EU's Industrial Accelerator Act, proposed in March, aims to pull manufacturing investment back to Europe by favoring EU-based firms in public contracts and subsidies.

Foreign investments in key sectors would only be approved if European partners keep majority control, which Beijing has framed as discriminatory.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

The European Automobile Manufacturers' Association (ACEA) warned last month that the draft act does little to counter the threat from cheaper Chinese rivals. In a position paper, it said the incentive to produce within the bloc has to be large enough to "cancel out the extra cost of producing locally."

Berlin's chief concern was that China could place new export curbs on rare earth minerals and the magnets made from them. China has a stranglehold on these elements, which are essential for German automotive, renewables and defense manufacturing.

Bloomberg last week cited unnamed German officials as saying that a new EU kill-switch could be a "second-strike weapon" if Beijing blocked those exports. Brussels is also considering unilateral limits on how many hybrid cars China can export to the EU, according to the same Bloomberg report.

Perhaps to avoid such an open confrontation, the EU and China reached a "shared understanding" last week at the EU-China trade talks in Beijing that could cut Chinese exports of hybrid and plug-in hybrid vehicles to the European Union by more than half, according to EU Trade Commissioner Maros Sefcovic, who headed the European delegation.

Reports say the agreement would cap such Chinese imports at 350,000 vehicles annually, with the limit increasing by 6% each year over four years.

Overall, new hybrid-electric cars in the EU reached nearly 37% of all new cars registered from January to August, according to ACEA data.

MERICS, meanwhile, calculated that the EU is a more critical export market for China than the US. In the first half of the year, Chinese exports to the EU were $254 billion (€354 billion), versus $172 billion to the US.

This could give EU negotiators a firmer hand as they seek to avoid a trade war while protecting Europe from China's latest export glut.

"The EU has more leverage than it sometimes thinks," MERICS' Mischer told DW.

#1040. Tottenham dealt latest attacking injury blow after VAR madness at Leeds

Please refresh the page or navigate to another page on the site to be automatically logged inPlease refresh your browser to be logged in

VAR spent over four minutes reviewing a possible red card offence when Jayden Bogle stamped on Tel’s ankle, but the challenge - which forced the Frenchman off - ultimately went unpunished

Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.

Tottenham have been dealt another attacking injury blow after Mathys Tel limped off before half-time against Leeds.

Tel was unable to continue after being on the end of a stamp by Jayden Bogle, who caught the Frenchman on the ankle with his studs.

VAR spent over four minutes reviewing the incident to determine whether it was a red card offence, only for referee John Brooks - who didn’t even caution Bogle initially - to be told to stick with the on-field decision. This meant the right wing-back got away with the challenge scot free.

“The referee’s call of no red card to Bogle for the challenge on Tel was checked and confirmed by VAR,” said the Premier League Match Centre.

The statement added VAR Tony Harrington’s verdict to Brooks: “I'm confirming the on-field decision of no red card. There’s a lack of speed going into the challenge and he’s stepping into the tackle. Confirming a reckless challenge”.

The challenge was similar to the one that saw Jean-Philippe Mateta shown red after a VAR review when Spurs played Crystal Palace last weekend.

Spurs manager Roberto De Zerbi was visibly frustrated with the outcome of the review and expressed his displeasure again when Pedro Porro was booked for a similar foul after the break, with the Italian booked for his reaction.

“Pedro Porro's was a duel and an incredible yellow card. The first situation of Mathys Tel I didn't see, I can't say nothing,” De Zerbi told TNT Sports, before stopping short of criticising the officials.

Asked if the referee should have gone to the monitor to review Bogle’s challenge, he said: "No. I have big confidence in the referee. Nothing changes if he goes to the monitor. If they didn't take the right decision I don't know. We have to keep the eyes on the performance where can improve."

Farke, meanwhile, insisted that Bogle would never have gone into the challenge with ill intent, branding his player a “butterfly”.

He said: “I have heard there were several doubtful situations. A possible hand ball. I just know that Jayden Bogle out of any bad intention. It looked like a coming together.

"It's very unlucky outcome that Mathys is injured and we wish him all the best and he can recover quickly. The last thing Jayden Bogle is a nasty player. He's possibly the softest player in the whole league. I always call him my butterfly, and I can guarantee it was never out of bad intention."

De Zerbi’s woes were exacerbated when Tel signalled to the bench that he would need to come off, having tried to play through the pain for five minutes.

Tel was replaced by Dominic Solanke in the 43rd minute, who was dropped from the starting line-up following the Palace win.

De Zerbi’s attacking options have already been ravaged by injury this season and the club will now be left to sweat over the extent of Tel’s setback.

De Zerbi said: “Tel has a bad injury on his ankle, but I don't know how long [he will be out] yet."

Savio and Mykhailo Mudryk are out until after the international break, while Xavi Simons and Wilson Odobert are continuing to work their way back from serious knee injuries, with both eyeing returns after the turn of the year.

Tel has impressed for Spurs in recent weeks, scoring a stunning solo goal in their 2-0 win over Chelsea on 24 October, the club’s first victory at Stamford Bridge since 2018.

#1039. How a once-controversial idea is advancing understanding of Parkinson’s disease

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Rachel Nuwer is a freelance writer based in New York City.

Microbiologist Sarkis Mazmanian says environmental factors often have a role in Parkinson’s.Credit: California Institute of Technology

Myriam Penninckx was having lunch at a restaurant in Brussels when her right arm began to shake. This was just the latest in a string of signs that something might be amiss. Her handwriting had suddenly become impossible to decipher, and she had noticed herself slowing down, physically and mentally. “I had always been Speedy Gonzales, doing a lot of things at the same time,” she says. “But that was becoming less possible.”

Penninckx was diagnosed with Parkinson’s disease shortly after her 60th birthday. She retired from her job and became depressed. “It was really hard to be someone who had a beautiful career, and then suddenly become a Parkinson’s patient,” she says. Her social life also ground to a halt. “If you have a tremor and you cannot cut your fish or eat your spaghetti, you don’t go out any more,” she says. “You close yourself to the world.”

When Penninckx heard about an unusual clinical trial being run at Ghent University in Belgium, she decided to enrol. In July 2021, she underwent a procedure that entailed flushing out her gut, and giving her a faecal transplant from a healthy donor to replace the community of microorganisms living there. The results, she says, “were amazing”. Her arm tremor went away and has not returned. She feels like the trial gave her “another shot at life”.

It might, at first, sound counterintuitive that such microbiome-targeting treatment could have marked benefits for people with Parkinson’s. Physicians have long been taught that the disease is a brain disorder that affects mainly the dopamine system, and that the hallmarks of the disease are Lewy bodies — misfolded clumps of a protein called α-synuclein that build up in neurons. But scientists have realized that the rest of the body is also involved, and the gut, in particular. For many individuals with Parkinson’s, evidence points to the gut’s involvement in the disease many years before diagnosis, says Per Borghammer, a neuroscientist at Aarhus University in Denmark.

Changes in the microbiome are also linked to some early symptoms and faster progression of the disease. These observations suggest that there are different subtypes of Parkinson’s, adds Filip Scheperjans, a neurologist at Helsinki University Hospital.

The gut’s seemingly central role in many Parkinson’s cases has implications not only for a better understanding of the disease’s origins and biology but also for tailoring treatments to an individual’s profile. “I make the comparison with what we see in oncology and cancer research,” says Arnout Bruggeman, the neurologist at Ghent University Hospital who oversaw Penninckx’s faecal transplant. Recognizing that various cancers exist as subtypes has allowed scientists to design vastly better treatments, he says — something he hopes will also be the case for Parkinson’s.

Hints that the gut is involved in Parkinson’s have been around since the disease was first described. People commonly have gastrointestinal issues, which sometimes start years before diagnosis. In 2003, researchers suggested that the α-synuclein pathology seen in the central nervous system might originate at peripheral sites, including the gut1. The work “introduced the idea that Parkinson’s disease starts very localized and then spreads via the neural connections”, Borghammer says. “It’s a little analogous to cancer that starts in one place and then metastasizes.”

Dozens of papers subsequently revealed that the microbiomes of people with Parkinson’s differ from those of people without the disease. In 2016, Sarkis Mazmanian, a microbiologist at the California Institute of Technology in Pasadena, showed that the microbiome plays a crucial part in the development of Parkinson’s-like symptoms in mice engineered to overexpress α-synuclein2. The animals’ symptoms went away when the researchers obliterated their microbiomes, and returned when they restored them. The team also transplanted human microbiomes into the mice, and found that rodents that received transplants from people with Parkinson’s had worse symptoms than did those who received transplants from healthy people.

In 2019, Borghammer and his colleague proposed that Parkinson’s can be divided into two main subtypes, according to where α-synuclein originates3. The ‘brain first’ subtype of the disease, he says, starts in the olfactory bulb, whereas a ‘body first’ version starts in the gut. This idea was controversial at first, and some researchers are still sceptical. But after years of mounting evidence, most are coming around to the idea.

Body-first Parkinson’s is thought to progress faster, and often manifests first with disturbances to the REM stage of sleep, gastrointestinal issues, depression, loss of smell and damage to the nerves that supply the heart (see ‘Teasing out distinct origins’). Brain-first Parkinson’s, by contrast, usually begins with motor symptoms. Eventually the subtypes converge — the end stage of the disease is the same, Borghammer says, it just starts in different places.

Source: P. Borghammer J. Neural Transm. 130, 737–753 (2023).

For both brain-first and body-first subtypes, the majority of Parkinson’s cases are attributable to “something you came across in your life”, Mazmanian says. Environmental risk factors seem to include air pollution, heavy metals, pesticides, certain viral infections and possibly microplastics.

Genes also play a part, however, and there is no bright-line distinction between genetic and environmental causes; the two are often linked. Variants of a gene called GBA1 are most closely associated with body-first Parkinson’s. But only a minority of carriers of the gene actually develop the disease, leading researchers to wonder what external factors might also have a role.

A study in April explored the part that the microbiome might play in increasing that risk, by examining hundreds of participants in the United Kingdom and Italy who did and did not have Parkinson’s, and likewise did and did not have a GBA1 variant linked to the disease4. The researchers analysed the participants’ stool samples and confirmed that the microbiomes of people with Parkinson’s differed significantly from those of people without the disease, and that the more severe the participant’s disease, the more altered was their microbiome. Mirroring earlier findings in mice, they also confirmed that, regardless of whether they carried a variant, people with Parkinson’s had roughly the same altered microbiome. This suggests that the disease process does more to transform a gut microbiome than do a person’s genes, says Elisa Menozzi, a clinical neuroscientist now at Aarhus University, and a co-author of the study.

As they had expected, Menozzi and her colleagues also found that healthy people carrying a GBA1 variant had, on average, microbiomes shifted toward the Parkinson’s pattern. But given that both carriers and non-carriers who already had Parkinson’s had statistically indistinguishable microbiomes, it seems that the variant itself is not what drives this change. Furthermore, in healthy participants not every carrier had this microbiome shift, and carriers who showed early, subtle signs of disease had microbiomes that looked most like those of people with Parkinson’s. Roughly one in five healthy participants without the variant also had the same altered microbiomes and signs that could be early markers of disease. The researchers’ interpretation, Menozzi says, is that changes to the microbiome raise the risk of Parkinson’s independently of genetics.

Taken together, Menozzi says, the findings suggest that the microbiome could be a diagnostic marker of Parkinson’s before symptoms become noticeable. Confirming this will require following the participants over time to see whether any of them develop Parkinson’s — something the team is doing, says co-author Anthony Schapira, a neurologist at University College London.

Although the study did not address what is causing the microbiome to change, the researchers found a significant association with participants’ eating habits. Diets that were high in vegetables, fruits and polyunsaturated fats seemed to protect against a Parkinson’s-type microbiome, whereas those high in saturated fat and low in fibre were associated with a microbiome closer to that of someone with the disease-altered microbiome. So dietary intervention is worth investigating, Schapira says. “The first question to answer is, can you do anything about this — can you change the microbiome?” he says. “ The next question is, does it matter?”

Some evidence from human trials already indicates that harnessing the microbiome to treat Parkinson’s could be possible. When Penninckx told her family that she would be receiving a faecal transplant as part of a study, she encountered some scepticism. “My grandchildren said, ‘Are you going to eat it?’” she recalls. She was relieved that was not the case. Instead, the researchers inserted a plastic tube into her nose, snaking it through her stomach and into her small intestine. “You’re never in contact with the material, so it’s not like there is a bad smell or taste,” she says.

Penninckx was one of 22 participants in the 2024 study to receive a faecal transplant from a healthy donor, while another 24 people were given a placebo made up of their own gut flora5. Twelve months after treatment, those who received the active treatment had fewer motor symptoms and less constipation than did those in the control group. The researchers plan to launch a larger trial this autumn to replicate these findings, Bruggeman says. Future trials will also analyse the composition of the microbiomes of healthy donors, which he says is “a key question” for determining the source of a potential positive effect.

Per Borghammer proposed that Parkinson’s can be divided into subtypes.Credit: Tonny Foghmar

Not all the results have been this promising. Scheperjans and his colleagues did not see a significant improvement in 30 participants who received an active treatment in a double-blind, placebo-controlled faecal transplant trial6. They do not know why their results differed from those in Belgium, but they suspect it might have had something to do with the method of delivery. The team administered treatment into the colon of participants rather than into the small intestine, which contains more immune cells than the large intestine. “It may be that for immune-system regulation, the small bowel is more important,” he says.

Surprisingly, the placebo group in this trial experienced more benefits than did the active treatment group. Up to 12 months after treatment, those in the placebo group had less constipation and more relief of some motor symptoms, as well as more changes to their microbiomes. The researchers think that this might be related to the bowel cleansing that all participants underwent before treatment — a hypothesis that they plan to test in a follow-up study. “If you have an abnormal microbiome, maybe the bowel cleansing gives you an opportunity to get recolonized with more normal bacteria,” Scheperjans says. “We’ll know if that’s the case after the next trial.”

Borghammer suspects that the differing faecal transplant results might come down to how “incredibly crude” the trials so far have been, simply because the field is so new. For example, researchers do not yet have the knowledge that would allow them to select the best donors for participants. Given this, he does not think that inconclusive results should be discouraging. “It’s plausible that it can work,” he says. “We just don’t understand it well enough yet.”

Another potential problem for faecal-transplant trials — and for research on Parkinson’s interventions in general — is that studies usually lump together people with body-first and brain-first subtypes. This could be confounding the results, Borghammer says, because different forms of the disease are likely to be driven by different mechanistic pathways. In 2022, for example, a phase III trial of an immunotherapy treatment targeting α-synuclein failed to produce significant results. But when the researchers later analysed the data for participants only with the most severe Parkinson’s, they found that the treatment did seem to slow progression of motor symptoms7. “It looks like for the fast-progressing type, which is strongly associated with the body-first type, it might have actually worked,” Borghammer says. “But because the original study included a mixed group of unselected patients, the clinical trial might have been unable to show statistically significant results.”

Myriam Penninckx was diagnosed with Parkinson’s disease shortly after turning 60.Credit: Courtesy of Myriam Penninckx

Researchers are increasingly aware of these limitations, and some groups are looking more closely at the bacterial species and mechanisms involved — and at more targeted populations. Haydeh Payami, a geneticist at the University of Alabama at Birmingham, and her team found that the gut microbiomes of about one-quarter of people with Parkinson’s contain high levels of a protein that induces aggregation of α-synuclein8. That protein is produced only by the bacterium Escherichia coli, giving scientists “one defined target”, says Mazmanian, who collaborates with Payami. Vertero Therapeutics, a firm Mazmanian co-founded in Woburn, Massachusetts, have developed a drug that inhibits production of the E. coli protein, and in mice it prevented α-synuclein from aggregating. “You can just stop this process in its tracks,” Mazmanian says.

In May, Vertero began a phase I trial in people with Parkinson’s whose microbiome matches the bacterial profile targeted by the drug. “In the population that we can treat, our hope is to slow down or even stop Parkinson’s progression,” Mazmanian says. “That would be a huge victory.”

The ultimate goal, however, is to be able to identify people in the very early stages of the disease, and then use pharmaceuticals, faecal transplants, dietary changes or other interventions to alter their trajectory. “Fast forward a decade, I hope we’ll be able to treat people before they actually develop Parkinson’s,” Mazmanian says.

Five years on, Penninckx still feels empowered by the gains she experienced in the faecal-transplant trial. She keeps busy as a board member of Parkili, a Belgian charity that supports scientific research — including some of Bruggeman’s work — and arranges trips around the world for people with Parkinson’s. She has travelled to Jordan with the group, and in May, she and seven others represented it at the World Parkinson’s Conference in Phoenix, Arizona. “I’ve started a new life,” she says. “So my story is a happy one.”

Penninckx knows that her disease is not cured. But her experience hints at the potential benefits that the mounting appreciation of the Parkinson’s gut–brain connection could bring.

#1038. Khadija Shaw’s hat-trick leads dominant Man City to victory over West Ham

Please refresh the page or navigate to another page on the site to be automatically logged inPlease refresh your browser to be logged in

City moved to the top of the WSL table with the win after Chelsea drew with Everton

Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.

Khadija Shaw continued her fine goalscoring form as she hit a hat-trick in Manchester City’s thumping 5-0 victory over West Ham at the Joie Stadium.

The Women’s Super League top scorer opened the scoring six minutes before the break with the only goal of the first half.

City then ran riot after the interval and put the Hammers to the sword, with four more goals as Shaw grabbed another couple for the match ball alongside strikes from Iman Beney and Aoba Fujino for their first goals of the campaign.

West Ham were happy to sit in and soak up the pressure from their opponents, and Constance Picaud-Inconnu got away with one when she parried Kerstin Casparij’s effort straight back into danger but no one was on hand to tap home.

The visitors had the woodwork to thank for not going a goal down when Fujino blasted off the near post.

It seemed only a matter of time before City made the breakthrough and they did just that five minutes before the break.

Hemp stole possession as the Hammers tried to play out from the back and the ball was worked to Shaw, who expertly dispatched.

City doubled their advantage eight minutes after the break has Shaw directed Hemp’s cross on goal with a header that Picaud-Inconnu was unable to keep out.

Fujino hit the crossbar but was not to be denied minutes later when she slotted across goal to put Manchester City three goals to the good.

Beney added a fourth for City just five minutes after stepping off the bench with a deflected strike from the edge of the box.

City were scoring at will and Shaw got her hat-trick with 16 minutes to play when she latched onto a through ball from Grace Clinton before grabbing her 12th goal from nine WSL games.

The victory sent City to the top of the table as, elsewhere, previous league leaders Chelsea had to settle for a 1-1 draw against Everton.

Sandy Baltimore had given Sonia Bompastor’s side the lead in the 28th minute having been set up beautifully by a Lucy Bronze header back across the penalty before a bizarre own goal from Bronze handed a leveller back to Everton just five minutes later.

Bronze had tried to clear the ball as it came into the area from the right side but a miscue saw the ball deflect off her heel and finish in the back of the Chelsea net.

The visitors held on for a draw as Chelsea dropped points for the first time since the opening day of the season handing the advantage in the title race to City.

#1037. Spurs to make formal complaint over Jayden Bogle decision

Tottenham Hotspur will make a formal complaint to Pro Ref over the decision not to send off Leeds United full-back Jayden Bogle for a foul that forced Mathys Tel off the pitch.

Bogle was penalised by John Brooks in the first half for treading on Tel’s foot before colliding with the French forward’s knee, but he was not shown either a yellow or red card. VAR looked at the challenge, which resulted in Tel coming off minutes later, but did not deem it serious foul play.

Should Jason Bogle have seen red for this challenge? 🟥👀 📺 Stream live on TNT Sports & HBO Max https://t.co/fRCRh6tXYB https://t.co/fuK42Okkcz

The explanation of the decision was played to the Elland Road crowd, which saw Leeds eventually win 1-0 through Noah Okafor’s goal.

“I’m confirming the on-field decision of no red card. There’s a lack of speed going into the challenge and he’s stepping into the tackle. Confirming a reckless challenge,” VAR Tony Harrington was quoted as saying on the big screen.

Spurs believe Bogle should have been sent off and will write to the refereeing body for an explanation, while head coach Roberto De Zerbi was upset with Brooks for booking Pedro Porro in the second half for a similar tackle.

Leeds head coach Daniel Farke said: “I haven’t watched the scenes back so I can’t give you a clear opinion, out of the game it looked a handball but the scene with Jayden was not too far away from my bench and it looked a very unlucky coming together.

“Fingers crossed for Mathys that he is back soon but it looked like there was not much speed in this action but Jayden Bogle is one of the most fair players in the country, he would never injure or foul a player on purpose because he is such a fair character.”

Tottenham Hotspur’s purple patch of form ended with a worrying loss. Wearing their “Spurple” kit for the first time, Roberto De Zerbi highlighted a lack of character and personality from his players and refused to blame the defeat on referee John Brooks’s decision not to dismiss Jayden Bogle for leaving one of his players injured.

Spurs’ away strip is based on a 1990s design, but this performance was more Christian Gross than Jürgen Klinsmann or David Ginola. Leeds United created the better chances and eventually broke through with 11 minutes remaining when their substitutes combined for Noah Okafor to score the winning goal.

Noah Okafor came off the bench and broke the deadlock just minutes later ⛓️‍💥 What a finish 🎯 📺 Stream live on TNT Sports & HBO Max https://t.co/fRCRh6tXYB https://t.co/pnbTQM1YpM

After victories against Coventry City, Chelsea and Crystal Palace, this was a blow for De Zerbi after looking to move Spurs into the European places. Leeds had not scored in 298 minutes of football, nor had they won in five previous matches, yet the Tottenham manager could barely recognise the players who had won three matches in a row.

De Zerbi had warned his team they would face a hostile atmosphere at Elland Road, but instead of rising to the challenge, Spurs were passive until it was too late.

“We didn’t win any duels, we didn’t win any one-to-ones, there was space to play and we didn’t take the right position,” De Zerbi said. “We didn’t show personality, we didn’t show what we are or who we are. It is part of the journey for sure. It can be normal in football but we have to be honest, if you are not honest the future is not good. If you analyse our behaviour we can become a top team.

“We worked very hard this week. We spoke all the days about the intensity, the type of game we would have found in this stadium and the atmosphere, it was not a surprise for us. Sometimes it can happen that we didn’t play the kind of game we want.”

De Zerbi’s honesty shines a light on the amount of work that still needs to be done at Spurs. Even after three straight wins, he has refused to get carried away despite fans looking upwards towards the European places.

Neither did the Italian want to blame the officials for failing to send off Bogle. Brooks has history with Spurs, sending off Xavi Simons against Liverpool last season. Here, he booked De Zerbi for his protests after Bogle’s heavy challenge that forced Mathys Tel off through injury.

Bogle trod on his opponent’s foot before clattering into his knee, forcing the French forward off a few minutes later. “I know that Jayden doesn’t foul out of bad intentions, he is not a nasty player and is one of the softest players in the whole league,” Leeds head coach Daniel Farke said. “I call him my butterfly.”

De Zerbi admitted the injury was “bad” and that Tel would now be scanned to determine the extent of the problem. The Spurs boss was upset that Pedro Porro was later booked for a similar challenge, while Bogle went unpunished – but he said the referee was not the cause of the defeat.

“I was surprised because in the same position in the second half there were two different fouls, the yellow card for Pedro Porro is not possible. I don’t know if it is a red card or not on Mathys Tel but the parameter of the referee was not good enough for this in both situations,” De Zerbi said.

Okafor was only on the pitch for 97 seconds before he finished off a move made by Farke’s replacements. Half-time substitute Melvin Bard sent a throw-in to Harry Wilson, who had also just come on and Okafor did the rest, bursting past Rodrigo Bentancur and planting his finish into the bottom corner. It meant the home fans were singing their “I Predict A Riot” winning anthem for just the second time this season.

For Leeds, moving into the top half will lift their own hopes of challenging for Europe, such is the congested mid-table.

“For us it has been a difficult period, we are missing key players like Anton Stach, Noah, Dominic [Calvert-Lewin] has not had the easiest spell with several injury problems and it was important to show this unity and commitment to avoid all their individual quality to score goals and reduce them to very little,” Farke added.

“Our final third, the quality was perhaps not there but second half there was no doubt just one team was pushing for that win. Another clean sheet another terrific defensive behaviour.”

Archie Gray will make his first appearance against his old club today after joining Spurs from Leeds in 2024. He was an unused sub in the two matches last season but is now an established part of this De Zerbi resurgence, starting all but two matches in the current campaign. Gray was named in the England Under-21 squad yesterday but is heading in the right direction for a senior call-up.

Dominic Calvert-Lewin is starting for Leeds today, after doubts over a foot issue heading into the Elland Road fixture. He was named in the England squad yesterday, which suggested he was not ruled out of this clash against Spurs

Roberto De Zerbi has kept a settled team as he looks to make it four Premier League wins in a row. Dominic Solanke is dropped to the bench in his only change, with Pedro Porro coming in – so it may be Omar Marmoush playing as a central forward.

There are many processes in [Tottenham’s] build-up. You need players to interpret this and the legs to cover the centre of the game. It is always complicated [tactically against a De Zerbi team], very dominant in possession. You have to find solutions to be competitive in this area.

The most important thing is what happens on the pitch but [we have bought] Sean [in because of the] tactical aspect. He is sop smart, has experience and also the legs to compete. It’s necessary to have a third midfielder on the pitch to control their processes. On the other hand he is sharp on the offensive actions, many times. Lukas [Nmecha] brings the greediness, physicality and can take the attention off Dominic. he has been very sharp in training, scoring many goals and for that he has the chance to shine today.

Dominic is a key player and thank God he was able to join us in team training yesterday. Overall he is in a good position.

You will always have spells in the Premier League when you cannot convert good performances into results or when you can’t score many goals. We are struggling with injuries for key players in our attack – Noah Okafor, Anton Stach – but hopefully we have also turned the corner.

The pre-season, it was clear [he is] a special talent. You recognise the special talent immediately and he doesn’t need to show something special, you understand? Everything that he does and he is one of the special talents.

The next step he has to enjoy, he has to follow the older players, the players with more experience like [Andrew] Robertson, [James] Maddison, Ben Davies and to find the time to play.

It is my responsibility because when you manage young players and sucho big talents like Luca, it is a bigger responsibility for me.

He has to be ready when he goes on the pitch. I think it [does] not depend on the result, he can play from the beginning. Before the Chelsea game, I thought to play with him in the first XI, but in the end you have to find the right moment and for them also.

I think the age is not so important. The most important is the quality, personality, the behaviour on the pitch and the qualities. And Luca has all of these qualities.

Leeds United are heartbroken to learn of the passing of supporter Colin Westby at the age of 68. Colin suffered a medical emergency ahead of our Premier League fixture with Manchester United on Sunday 18 October at Elland Road. After being transferred to hospital, he was placed into a medically induced coma and sadly following a period of unresponsiveness, the decision was made to withdraw life support. Colin was a long-standing Season Ticket Holder at the club, attending matches for over 50 years. The thoughts of everyone at Leeds United are with Colin's family and friends at this sad time. We will pay tribute to Colin in the 68th minute of our next Premier League fixture with Tottenham Hotspur, on Saturday 7 November.

Good morning and welcome to live coverage of the Premier League match between Leeds United and Tottenham Hotspur at Elland Road. The home side, lions at night and mice in the morning, have the unenviable record of 21 top-flight matches with a kick-off time before 3pm without a win. All that extra TV moolah comes in handy but their home ground, a bearpit under the floodlights, is neutered when its denizens are yawning instead of being fired up by social lubricant.

Daniel Farke’s team started the campaign well but are now without a win in five, drawing three matches with teams beneath them in the table – Crystal Palace, Manchester United and Sunderland – and  losing to two above them, Arsenal and Bournemouth. In fairness they played well against the champions for an hour and were deservedly in the lead until Mikel Arteta turnd to his billionaire’s bench and changed the game. At Bournemouth last week they also made a decent start, had a goal disallowed for striking Dominic Calvert-Lewin’s arm and then James Trafford chucked one in.

They never recovered, found themselves increasingly bogged down when trying to unlock a low block and were mugged on the break in added time to lose 2-0. They are a robust side overly reliant on their wing-backs to create chances for their No 9 in the absence of the injured Noah Okafor who was unavailable to train with the team this week because of a groin injury but may be fit enough for the bench.

Spurs, by contrast, are buoyant following three wins on the bounce – over Coventry, Chelsea and Palace, two with clean sheets – that has taken them from 19th to ninth, three places above Leeds. They have won their last three visits to Elland Road, 0-4 under Antonio Conte, which proved to be the last match of Marcelo Bielsa’s glorious spell at the Peacocks, 1-4 under Ryan Mason, which sealed Leeds’ relegation, and 1-2 under Tomas Frank last year by virtue of goals from Mathys Tel and Mohammed Kudus as the home side struggled against their width back in the days before their switch to a back three.

Tel also scored in Spurs’ home game, a 1-1 draw in May, and then kicked Ethan Ampadu in the head to concede the penalty from which Leeds equalised. I wonder what kind of impact he will have today. Incidentally Roberto De Zerbi on his last visit to Leeds when manager of Brighton in 2022-23 had such a strop on the touchline when the home team equalised that he was within a gnat’s whisker of being sent off.
